articles.title: Watch Trump compare Natalie Harp to 'Price is Right' presenter
articles.summary: Trump, who was campaigning in Nebraska ahead of the November midterm elections, called Natalie Harp to bring an executive order onto the stage.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is likening Natalie Harp to a " Price is Right " presenter.

"She reminds me like the 'Price is Right'," Trump said as the White House aide walked off the stage at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska on Monday, Oct. 5, holding the executive order he had just signed.

He continued: "Come on. This perfect person comes up, hands it, walks off. We should go on television with this show, right?"

Watch the moment in the video at the top of this story.

The president, who was campaigning for incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts and Gov. Jim Pillen ahead of the November midterm elections, called the White House aide to bring an executive order temporarily allowing broader access to tax-free diesel fuel , crucial for trucking and agriculture onto the stage.

He then teased the audience before taking a dig at former President Joe Biden , saying he's "going to do what Joe Biden couldn't do. Sign his signature."

He signed the order, showed it off to the crowd and then tossed the Sharpie into the cheering audience.

Trump's new executive order defers collection of excise tax on so-called red dye diesel fuel through the end of the year. The fuel is dyed because it is typical for off-road uses such as agriculture and is exempt from federal highway taxes. The president said the order would save truckers an average of $100 each time they fill up and will save farmers millions of dollars.

Take a look at Natalie Harp’s life alongside Donald Trump

Natalie Harp , an aide to President Trump, listens as Trump announces Dulles International Airport renovations in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC on July 29, 2026. Her name came up recently as she was chosen to accompany the president when he was secretly removed from Air Force One and transferred to another plane via an airline catering truck amid threats on the president's life from Iran.

"The Price is Right," which airs on CBS, is the network television's number one rated daytime series "and the longest-running game show in television history," according to its website . The show, on which audience members try to win cash and prizes, is hosted by Drew Carey.

The show is known for its slate of models, mostly women, that present the prizes to contestants.

Harp, 34, is Trump's executive assistant and one of the most visible figures in the president's inner circle. A former television presenter for One America News Network, Harp graduated from Point Loma Nazarene University in 2012 and received an MBA from Liberty University in 2015, according to Vanity Fair .

Harp first gained national attention after crediting Trump's "Right to Try" law with helping her access an experimental treatment for bone cancer , according to Forbes. She spoke at the 2020 Republican National Convention and later worked on Trump's 2024 presidential campaign before joining the White House as executive assistant at the start of his second term.

Harp has become known in Trump circles as the " human printer ," a nickname tied to her habit of carrying a portable printer and battery pack so she could provide the president with physical copies of information wherever he traveled, according to reporting by The Palm Beach Post , part of the USA TODAY Network.

She has also been linked in reports to some of Trump's most controversial social media activity through her access to his Truth Social account.

Harp is a survivor of bone cancer and has frequently spoken about how the experimental treatment she received under the "Right to Try" program affected her life.

The law, signed by Trump in 2018, allows some terminally ill patients to seek access to treatments that have not yet received full approval from the Food and Drug Administration.

Saman Shafiq is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at sshafiq@usatodayco.com and follow her on X and Instagram @saman_shafiq7.

articles.title: Cid Gomes defende fim da escala 6x1 e comenta relação com Ciro | G1
articles.standfirst: Cid Gomes foi entrevistado ao vivo no CE1 nesta quarta-feira (7). Ele projetou seu novo mandato e comentou estratégias eleitorais para o segundo turno.
articles.summary: O senador reeleito Cid Gomes analisa o rompimento político com Ciro, apoia a redução da jornada de trabalho e detalha a mobilização pró-Lula no Ceará.
articles.body:
O senador Cid Gomes (PSB) , reeleito pelo Ceará no último domingo (4) com 31,22% dos votos, concedeu entrevista ao CE1, da TV Verdes Mares, nesta quarta-feira (7). Na conversa, ele falou sobre desafios e propostas para o novo mandato.

Cid é o primeiro senador reeleito pelo Ceará desde a redemocratização. Em 2018, foi eleito pela primeira vez para o cargo, com a maior votação já registrada por um candidato no estado até então.

Entre os principais temas abordados na entrevista estão a relação com o irmão, Ciro Gomes, o debate sobre o fim da escala 6x1 e estratégias para ampliar a votação do presidente Lula no segundo turno das eleições, marcado para 25 de outubro. Veja os principais trechos:

Cid Gomes comenta relação com Ciro, defende fim da escala 6x1 e fala sobre estratégia para Lula no 2º turno. — Foto: Fabiane de Paula/Sistema Verdes Mares (SVM)

Ciro tem 'direito de espernear', diz Cid sobre irmão entrar na Justiça contra eleição

Ao comentar a reação do irmão, Ciro Gomes (PSDB), à derrota na disputa pelo governo do Ceará para Elmano de Freitas (PT), Cid afirmou que teria sido mais elegante reconhecer o resultado e cumprimentar o governador eleito.

Após as eleições de domingo (4), Ciro declarou que o pleito no estado foi “tomado” e afirmou que apresentaria uma “reclamação à Justiça” sobre a disputa no Ceará .

Ao g1 , a assessoria de imprensa de Ciro informou que o tucano pretende pedir a anulação da eleição para o governo do estado. Cid criticou a postura do irmão, mas disse que ele tem o “direito de espernear”.

“O papai era advogado e tem uma expressão do latim, muito usada no direito, que é o jus sperniandi . Uma tradução livre é o direito de espernear . Eu acho que teria sido mais elegante reconhecer a vitória, cumprimentar o governador, dizer qual seria a sua posição — se é uma posição de diálogo ou se é uma posição de oposição. Acho que isso seria mais elegante, seria o que eu teria feito no lugar.”

➡️ A expressão "jus sperniandi" é um termo informal e utilizada em tom de brincadeira. A palavra "sperniandi" não existe em latim, é apenas um trocadilho para parecer uma expressão latina, muito comum nos termos jurídicos.

Questionado se conversou com Ciro após o pleito e se pretende retomar a relação política com ele, Cid respondeu que a “relação familiar fica no plano da relação familiar”. Ele, no entanto, voltou a criticar alianças feitas pelo irmão durante a campanha ao governo do estado.

Na disputa, Ciro esteve ao lado de Capitão Wagner (União), derrotado na eleição para o Senado , e de André Fernandes (PL), deputado federal eleito .

“O Ciro se aliou ao Wagner, que é um permanente adversário nosso. O Ciro se aliou ao André Fernandes, que, a meu juízo, é um bolsonarista oco, que não tem nada a apresentar de projeto e que virou um fenômeno de uma coisa, a meu juízo, pouco crítica. Enquanto ele estiver nesse caminho, a gente não tem diálogo político. A relação familiar a gente deixa para o plano familiar".

Cid Gomes também comentou a proposta de redução da jornada de trabalho e defendeu o fim da escala 6x1. A Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) em tramitação no Senado prevê o fim do regime de seis dias consecutivos de trabalho para um de descanso.

➡️ Se aprovada, a medida garantiria aos trabalhadores dois dias de descanso por semana, sem redução salarial.

Favorável à proposta, o senador afirmou que a mudança não deve desacelerar a atividade econômica do país e disse que esse tema evidencia diferenças entre os candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT).

“Esse país já teve escravidão, já teve uma jornada de 48 horas. Hoje é 44 horas. Vai morrer a atividade econômica no Brasil se baixar para 40? Claro que não. Quem está do lado dos trabalhadores, para assegurar aos trabalhadores dois dias inteiros de descanso, é o presidente Lula. Quem está contra é o Flávio Bolsonaro. Os bolsonaristas todos são contra, ficam aí inventando conversas, dizendo que querem uma flexibilização da jornada.”

O tema é considerado estratégico para os dois candidatos que disputam o segundo turno da eleição presidencial, marcado para 25 de outubro. A PEC 221/2019 começou a ser debatida no plenário do Senado nesta terça-feira (6).

Cid Gomes se reuniu na segunda-feira (5), em Brasília, com o presidente Lula para discutir estratégias para o segundo turno. Segundo o senador, uma das principais conclusões do encontro foi a necessidade de reforçar o diálogo com eleitores da zona rural e com os idosos .

“A eleição tem sempre muitas ideias, muitas sugestões, e pode ter certeza de que apareceram sugestões de todas as formas. O que, a meu juízo, ficou meio conclusivo é que a gente deve reforçar um percentual de pessoas que não votaram e que geralmente são pessoas da zona rural, são pessoas de maior idade, que são potenciais simpatizantes da candidatura do Lula. Então, buscar esse tipo de eleitor".

A mobilização do PT no estado busca agora ampliar esse desempenho e ultrapassar os 70% dos votos para Lula no Ceará no segundo turno, como já declarou o governador reeleito Elmano de Freitas (PT).

“Acho que o presidente Lula tem que falar para o povo e deixar claro que o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro é o candidato dos ricos egoístas deste país, e ele é o candidato dos pobres, daqueles que querem ascender na vida, daqueles que querem melhorar, dos trabalhadores. É essa claramente a diferença, e isso vai ficar muito óbvio agora, semana que vem, quando vai ter a votação do fim da escala 6x1.”, declarou o senador Cid Gomes.

articles.title: Aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro alertam para risco de discurso sobre mudança na Constituição e clima de 'já ganhou' | G1
articles.body:
Aliados do candidato do PL à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro, alertam para o risco de declarações como a de mudar a Constituição para “redemocratizar o país” , que podem transmitir uma mensagem de autoritarismo. Também pedem que o senador evite adotar um tom de “já ganhou”.

Na avaliação desses interlocutores, o momento é favorável a Flávio Bolsonaro, que chegou ao segundo turno à frente de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), mas a diferença entre os dois candidatos ainda pode ser revertida.

Segundo aliados do senador, Flávio Bolsonaro adotou nesta terça-feira (6), em Goiânia, um tom de quem já se considerava eleito e começava a planejar as primeiras medidas de um eventual governo, entre elas mudanças na Constituição.

Desde a redemocratização, os candidatos que terminaram o primeiro turno à frente também venceram o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais ( leia mais abaixo ).

Interlocutores de Flávio, no entanto, avaliam que esse histórico não é garantia de vitória e consideram perigoso entrar na etapa final da disputa de “salto alto”.

Ao receber o apoio do ex-governador de Goiás, Ronaldo Caiado, Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou que um Congresso com maioria de direita permitiria fazer mudanças na Constituição para “redemocratizar o país”.

A declaração foi explorada por aliados do presidente Lula, que afirmaram que o candidato do PL estaria planejando medidas autoritárias capazes de colocar em risco regras democráticas.

Interlocutores de Flávio Bolsonaro buscaram explicar a declaração. Segundo eles, o candidato não pretende adotar medidas autoritárias e as cláusulas pétreas da Constituição não podem ser abolidas por emenda constitucional.

Entre as garantias protegidas estão o voto direto, secreto, universal e periódico; a separação dos Poderes; e os direitos e garantias individuais.

Na interpretação desses aliados, o senador queria sinalizar que, com uma maioria no Congresso, teria condições políticas de levar adiante propostas de campanha que dependem do Legislativo, como a redução da maioridade penal de 18 para 16 anos e mudanças no Judiciário.

Ronaldo Caiado e Flávio Bolsonaro, em Goiânia — Foto: Wildes Barbosa/O Popular

Nesta primeira semana do segundo turno, Flávio Bolsonaro saiu na frente na busca por apoios políticos.

Conseguiu as adesões de Ronaldo Caiado e Romeu Zema, além de União Brasil e Progressistas . Nesta quarta (7), Republicanos e Podemos podem seguir o mesmo caminho .

O candidato do PL busca atrair a maior parte dos 8% dos votos que foram destinados aos demais candidatos de direita no primeiro turno, parcela que pode ser decisiva para o resultado da eleição.

Na manhã desta quarta, Flávio Bolsonaro usou um tom mais moderado em sua fala, e prometeu respeito à Constituição.

O candidato afirmou ainda não ter procedência avaliações de que ele poderia adotar medidas autoritárias.

"Eu já vi gente começar a dizer: 'Ah, agora o Flávio com esse Congresso com ampla maioria ele vai fazer o que o pai dele não fez'. Vamos parar de mentir, vamos aterrizar no mundo real, para de fazer torcida", afirmou.

"Eu respeito o trabalho de todo mundo, mas são pessoas que são influentes, as vozes são ouvidas por alguns outros brasileiros na audiência deles ali. A ameaça que tem à democracia tem é com o Lula. Vocês estão vendo aí, gente. Não vai ter com Flávio Bolsonaro", prosseguiu.

Flávio reforçou que o Brasil tem que voltar ao normal e que, com ele no governo, o Brasil vai ter segurança jurídica e respeito à Constituição.

articles.title: Em novo vídeo, Lula cobra Flávio Bolsonaro sobre escala 6x1: 'Quero saber como vai votar' | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente voltou às redes sociais nesta quarta (7) e disse que fim da escala permitirá ao trabalhador ter mais tempo para descanso, lazer e convívio com a família.
articles.summary: Presidente voltou às redes sociais nesta quarta (7) e disse que fim da escala permitirá ao trabalhador ter mais tempo para descanso, lazer e convívio com a família.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , candidato do PT à reeleição, voltou a usar as redes sociais nesta quarta-feira (7), desta vez para cobrar uma posição do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), seu adversário no segundo turno, sobre o fim da escala de trabalho 6x1.

No vídeo, Lula questionou como Flávio Bolsonaro pretende se posicionar sobre a proposta e como vai orientar o PL, sigla da qual é filiado.

"Eu quero saber como é que o Flávio Bolsonaro vai votar. Eu quero saber como é que ele vai orientar o PL para votar", questionou.

A publicação ocorre no mesmo dia em que Lula divulgou outro vídeo, também nas redes sociais, no qual convocou apoiadores a irem às ruas e conversarem com eleitores para tentar vencer o segundo turno.

Após o resultado do primeiro turno, integrantes da campanha passaram a defender uma presença maior do presidente nas redes sociais para aumentar a base de alcance do petista.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT), que disputam o segundo turno presidencial no dia 25 de outubro — Foto: Vittor Sales e Ricardo Stuckert

No novo vídeo, Lula explicou a proposta como uma mudança de seis dias de trabalho e um de descanso para cinco dias de trabalho e dois de folga.

"Por que nós queremos que o trabalhador fique dois dias em casa? Para ele descansar mais, para ele poder viver mais com a família, para passear com os filhos, para visitar os parentes, para ele poder ter um pouco de lazer na sua vida", disse.

Lula afirmou ainda que a discussão da proposta permitirá aos eleitores conhecer a posição dos políticos sobre o tema.

"Agora chegou a hora do povo saber a verdade. Quem é quem nesse país", afirmou.

Nesta terça (6), Lula já havia voltado a defender o fim da escala 6x1 e afirmado que queria ver a redução da jornada "sair do papel". Na ocasião, o petista disse que Flávio Bolsonaro é contra a mudança.

"Flávio Bolsonaro é contra. Para ele, quem trabalhar menos tem que ganhar menos. Queria ver ele explicar para uma mãe de família qual conta ela deixa de pagar para poder descansar. A comida? A luz? O aluguel? Quem vive de salário sabe que isso não é escolha", disse Lula na terça.

A proposta em análise no Congresso estabelece jornada máxima de 40 horas semanais, divididas em cinco dias de trabalho e dois de descanso, sem redução salarial.

O plenário do Senado começou a discutir a PEC nesta terça. O presidente da Casa, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), indicou que a primeira votação pode ocorrer na próxima semana.

O texto já foi aprovado pela Câmara e pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado. Agora, precisa passar por dois turnos de votação no plenário do Senado.

Entre os governistas, a estratégia é tentar aprovar a proposta antes do segundo turno e expor o posicionamento de integrantes da oposição sobre a medida.

Já senadores aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro tentam evitar a votação dessa PEC e defendem que uma proposta alternativa seja analisada.

A discussão sobre o fim da escala 6x1começou terça (6), no plenário do Senado. A sessão teve discursos favoráveis à proposta e ausência da maioria dos senadores do PL. Flávio Bolsonaro também não participou da discussão.

Antes da sessão de terça, Alcolumbre havia mantido o calendário de discussão da proposta. Pelo rito do Senado, uma PEC precisa passar por cinco sessões de discussão antes da votação em primeiro turno. Na noite de terça, o presidente do Senado sinalizou que a votação poderá ocorrer na próxima semana.

articles.title: Flávio diz que fala sobre mudar a Constituição 'para redemocratizar o país' se referia à reforma do STF e fim da reeleição | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato adotou um tom mais moderado em respeito à Constituição. Ele também citou mudanças que pretende fazer na reforma tributária aprovada pelo Congresso.
articles.summary: Candidato adotou um tom mais moderado em respeito à Constituição. Ele também citou mudanças que pretende fazer na reforma tributária aprovada pelo Congresso.
articles.body:
O candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) afirmou, nesta quarta-feira (7), que a declaração sobre querer "mudar a Constituição para redemocratizar o país" se referia a propostas já anunciadas por ele caso seja eleito, como a redução da maioridade penal e mudanças no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ).

"Vocês acham que o Brasil está numa democracia plena? Não. A gente tem que respeitar a política, tem várias PECs [propostas de mudanças na Constituição] que são possíveis", disse.

“Tem que haver, sim, uma reforma no Judiciário. Eu sou a favor da redução da maioridade penal há bastante tempo, tem que ser feito por PEC. Tem pontos da reforma tributária que têm que ser alterados por PEC. E o fim da reeleição", prosseguiu.

"Comigo não vai ter isso, vai ter estabilidade, vai ter paz para todo mundo trabalhar, vai ter segurança jurídica, respeito à Constituição. Vai ser o normal. O Brasil tem que voltar ao normal".

Ele deu a declaração em Goiânia, ao lado do candidato derrotado no primeiro turno Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), que anunciou apoio à candidatura dele.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) — Foto: Foto: Vittor Sales

Questionado pela imprensa nesta quarta (7) sobre o que quis dizer com a declaração, o candidato adotou um tom mais moderado em respeito à Constituição, e tentou afastar qualquer possibilidade de medidas autoritárias.

"Comigo vai ser sempre com ponderação, com respeito à política e honrando e respeitando cada seguimento da sociedade aqui representado nesses parlamentares, não só os deputados estaduais e federais que estão aqui, mas os governadores, as candidatas ao governo que estão concorrendo ainda, os senadores", disse.

Ele também comentou críticas que a declaração vem sofrendo. "Eu já vi gente começar a dizer: 'Ah, agora o Flávio com esse Congresso com ampla maioria ele vai fazer o que o pai dele não fez [no caso da trama golpista]. Vamos parar de mentir, vamos aterrizar no mundo real".

A reforma do Judiciário já aparece no programa de governo de Flávio Bolsonaro, que reúne propostas principalmente relacionadas ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), entre elas mudanças em decisões monocráticas.

A redução da maioridade penal também já havia sido defendida pelo candidato. Em agosto, Flávio Bolsonaro afirmou que apoiaria a redução de 18 para 16 anos. A proposta em discussão no Congresso altera o artigo 228 da Constituição e, portanto, precisa ser aprovada por meio de uma PEC.

Flávio também disse que não pretende concorrer à reeleição, caso conquiste um mandato como presidente. Afirmou que a decisão caberá ao Congresso. O partido dele, PL, elegeu 121 deputados e conquistou a maior bancada na Câmara desde a Constituição de 1988.

"Quando eu falo que eu sou a favor do fim da reeleição e é assim que eu vou fazer, eu vou usar o capital político de um presidente recém-eleito para aprovar essa PEC para redemocratizar o nosso país nesse sentido. É para dar o exemplo", afirmou.

“Para mostrar que eu não estou disputando o poder como esse atual governo. [...] Não estou disputando o poder. Eu estou disputando o futuro do meu país, futuro para as minhas filhas, para as filhas de vocês que estão aqui, para quem está assistindo. Então, fiz o compromisso de não concorrer à reeleição".

Segundo Flávio Bolsonaro, a definição de como funcionaria o fim da reeleição ficaria a cargo dos deputados e senadores.

“É o Congresso que vai discutir os critérios, se vai ser mandato de quatro, de cinco anos, se vai valer só para presidente, se vai valer para governador. Aí é o processo legislativo que vai ser respeitado e a maioria vai decidir qual é o caminho que tem que ser feito, a reforma política.”

articles.title: Impeachment de ministros do STF: novo Senado pressiona Supremo | G1
articles.standfirst: Fontes ouvidas pelo blog dizem que o funcionamento do STF e possíveis pedidos de impeachment de ministros do Supremo são pautas das quais não vai dar para fugir. Sob pressão do novo Senado, movimentos de Moraes entram no radar da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.summary: Impeachment de ministros do STF e mudanças no Judiciário tornam-se pautas centrais após avanço da direita no Senado e articulações de Rogério Marinho.
articles.body:
Enquanto as campanhas do 2 º turno das eleições seguem na rua, um movimento acontece nos bastidores: as movimentações da nova composição do Senado em relação ao Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ).

Para a maioria dos novos eleitos, a principal bandeira de atuação no ano que vem é o funcionamento do STF e o impeachment de ministros.

O senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), que é coordenador da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), deu um giro no Supremo na última terça-feira (6). Nos bastidores, ele tem conversado com ministros e, principalmente, com o presidente do Supremo, ministro Edson Fachin .

A Fachin, Marinho tem dito que não haverá uma vingança ou revanche por parte do novo Senado — que terá 19 cadeiras só para o PL, formando a maior bancada da Casa. Mesmo assim, o Supremo tem monitorado o cenário.

Apesar das conversas com os ministros, Rogério Marinho não tem tido contato com os ministros Alexandre de Moraes e Flávio Dino. Moraes, na visão do campo conservador, é tido como o símbolo do anti-bolsonarismo. Com o novo Senado, que tem a maioria alinhada ao posicionamento do PL, os movimentos do ministro entram no radar da campanha de Flávio.

Integrantes do Judiciário ouvidos pelo blog dizem que nem todo bolsonarista é a favor do impeachment de ministros. Ainda assim, os parlamentares relatam que foram eleitos muito por conta dessa pauta e querem fazer jus às promessas de campanha.

Um outro ponto determinante para a relação entre Supremo e Senado é a escolha do próximo presidente da casa legislativa, cuja eleição se dará em fevereiro do ano que vem.

O próprio Rogério Marinho tem sido um dos nomes mais cotados pelas fontes ouvidas pelo blog , e a expectativa é que ele saia na frente até mesmo de Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), atual presidente do Senado. Ambas as campanhas presidenciais, de Flávio Bolsonaro e de Lula (PT), avaliam que Alcolumbre perde vantagem no atual cenário.

Alcolumbre é ligado à ala de Moraes no Supremo, e uma troca no comando do Senado pode colocar ainda mais pressão sobre o ministro.

Um terceiro nome que corre pelos bastidores para liderar o Senado é o de Arthur Lira (PP-AL), ex-presidente da Câmara e recém-eleito ao Senado. Fontes ouvidas pelo blog dizem que ele poderia representar uma liderança de meio de caminho, que consiga equilibrar as forças.

Uma coisa é unânime: neste novo Senado, ninguém vai conseguir fugir da pauta do Supremo.

articles.title: 231,5 mil eleitores apertaram '10' para presidente e anularam o voto | G1
articles.standfirst: Número do Republicanos só ficou atrás de '00' nos dados dos Registros Digitais de Voto (RDVs), do TSE. O '17', usado por Jair Bolsonaro em 2018, também aparece, assim como números de antigas candidaturas de Tebet, Ciro e Marina.
articles.summary: Número do Republicanos só ficou atrás de '00' nos dados dos Registros Digitais de Voto (RDVs), do TSE. O '17', usado por Bolsonaro em 2018, também aparece no levantamento do g1.
articles.body:
Demonstração do fluxo de votação das Eleições 2026, na sede do TRE-SP, centro da capital, SP. Na foto a urna eletrônica. — Foto: ROBERTO CASIMIRO/FOTOARENA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Mais de 231 mil eleitores digitaram e confirmaram o número 10 para presidente e, assim, acabaram por anular seus votos no primeiro turno das eleições de 2026 , segundo dados dos Registros Digitais de Voto (RDVs). O número 10 pertence ao Republicanos , mas não correspondia a nenhuma candidatura à Presidência nesta eleição.

Ao todo, foram identificados 231.492 votos nessas condições. O 10 só ficou atrás do 00, confirmado em 1.872.196 votos nulos. Na sequência, apareceu o 15, do MDB , com 230.598 registros.

O levantamento foi feito pelo g1 com dados dos Registros Digitais de Voto, do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), que reúne os números confirmados na urna e a quantidade de votos nulos para presidente no país.

🔎 Os Registros Digitais de Voto (RDVs) são arquivos da urna eletrônica que guardam cada voto confirmado , separado por cargo, incluindo os números digitados nos votos nulos. Os registros são embaralhados para preservar o sigilo: não permitem identificar quem votou nem associar os votos de uma mesma pessoa para cargos diferentes.

Não é possível saber se houve confusão do eleitor ou intenção de anular. A coincidência com o número de um partido ou de uma candidatura anterior não comprova em quem o eleitor pretendia votar.

O número 10 é de um dos principais aliados do candidato a presidente Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), o governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), que se reelegeu. Tarcísio foi cotado para concorrer à Presidência, mas Flávio acabou escolhido por Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

Entre os votos nulos para presidente no primeiro turno, aparecem números que fizeram parte de campanhas presidenciais anteriores. O 15, terceiro mais frequente, foi usado por Simone Tebet em 2022 e por Henrique Meirelles em 2018, ambos pelo MDB.

O 17, com o qual Jair Bolsonaro disputou e venceu a eleição presidencial de 2018 pelo PSL, apareceu em 7.925 votos nulos. O partido se fundiu com o DEM em 2022 para formar o União Brasil , que utiliza o número 44.

12 — 164.538 votos nulos: número do PDT , usado por Ciro Gomes em 2018 e 2022.

44 — 114.387 votos: número do União Brasil, usado por Soraya Thronicke em 2022.

45 — 95.605 votos: número do PSDB , usado por Aécio Neves em 2014 e Geraldo Alckmin em 2018.

40 — 92.752 votos: número do PSB , usado por Marina Silva em 2014.

20 — 53.907 votos: atualmente do Podemos , foi usado por Pastor Everaldo , então no PSC, em 2014.

50 — 29.685 votos: número do PSOL, usado por Luciana Genro em 2014 e Guilherme Boulos em 2018.

18 — 26.851 votos: número da Rede, usado por Marina Silva em 2018.

Há ainda registros com números de partidos que passaram por mudanças. O 25, confirmado em 16.707 votos nulos, pertence hoje ao PRD, mas já identificou o DEM. O 51, com 5.027 registros, foi usado por Cabo Daciolo em 2018 pelo Patriota, partido que posteriormente se fundiu com o PTB para formar o PRD.

Ao todo, os registros reúnem 3.624.443 votos nulos distribuídos por 87 combinações de dois dígitos. O 00 concentra 51,7% dos registros. Veja os dez números mais frequentes :

A identificação das legendas segue o cadastro do TSE. 00 e 99 não correspondem a partidos registrados.

Votos nulos e em branco nas eleições 2026

Na disputa presidencial, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) vão se enfrentar no segundo turno , em 25 de outubro. Flávio recebeu cerca de 56,1 milhões de votos, ou 47,03% dos válidos, enquanto Lula teve 53,9 milhões, equivalentes a 45,16%. A diferença foi de aproximadamente 2,2 milhões de votos.

A eleição de 2026 registrou 3.674.249 votos nulos , equivalentes a 2,93% dos votos apurados, e 2.300.798 votos em branco , ou 1,84%. Juntas, as duas categorias somaram quase 6 milhões de votos , que não entram no cálculo dos votos válidos.

Outros 33.469.244 eleitores não compareceram às urnas. A taxa de abstenção foi de 21,08%, a maior em um primeiro turno de eleição geral desde 1998 , quando 21,49% dos eleitores deixaram de votar.

articles.title: Congress killed the penny — now it's coming for the 13-cent nickel
articles.summary: The Common Cents Act already targets the penny, but lawmakers now want the Treasury Department to find cheaper ways to produce the nickel coin.
articles.body: It's common sense that common cents are getting less use in Americans' daily lives. Congress has already taken action to eliminate the lowest rung — the penny — and now another coin collecting dust in people's wallets could be on the chopping block next. The House and Senate both passed bills earlier this year aimed at eliminating the penny once and for all. The bipartisan Common Cents Act was unanimously approved in each chamber, but has yet to get President Donald Trump's signature to become law. It followed the Treasury Department announcing last December that the U.S. Mint would no longer produce pennies, which at the time cost more than three times their value to make. TRUMP’S FIRST-YEAR GOVERNMENT OVERHAUL DELIVERS CHANGE WASHINGTON HASN’T SEEN SINCE THE 1960S Now, lawmakers want the administration to act on another portion of their bill, which would direct the Treasury to study the potential of making the nickel with cheaper materials than are currently used. "If it costs 13 cents to make a five-cent coin, Washington should fix the problem instead of wasting more taxpayer money," House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. "My bill gives Treasury a path to make nickels at a lower cost without disrupting how Americans use them. It is a simple reform that saves money and brings a little more common sense to government." Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., who led the bill in the Senate, told Fox News Digital, "More and more Americans are paying with credit cards, debit cards and stablecoins for everyday purchases that once would have been made with cash or coins." "The half-cent coin was retired when it was no longer needed, and the penny has now reached that same point. It’s my hope that we can find a cheaper way to produce the nickel so that it remains economically viable for years to come," Lummis said. Nickels are produced at a loss to taxpayers of roughly eight cents per coin, according to the latest data. They are currently made of a mixture comprised of 25% nickel and 75% copper. The Common Cents Act "authorizes a lower-cost nickel composition if testing shows it will reduce production costs without significantly disrupting coin-operated machines," such as vending machines, according to a release on McClain's site. But it's not clear that there is much appetite for ending nickel production altogether, at least not yet. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News in May 2025 that he believed the U.S. could "retool" the nickel to make it cheaper to produce. In its December 2025 announcement, the Trump administration projected immediate cost savings of $56 million in stopping penny minting. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the decision could be reversed by any future administration unless Trump signs the bill into law. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on whether and when the president plans to do so.

articles.title: Ex-Obama spy chief prepped for anti-Trump trial by Biden-era special counsel's team, new records reveal
articles.summary: Declassified FBI memo reveals Jack Smith's team met with Trump-critic and former CIA Director John Brennan to discuss Trump's case, despite Smith telling GOP lawmakers he had never met Brennan before.
articles.body: Former special counsel Jack Smith told lawmakers he had "never met" former CIA director and vocal Trump critic John Brennan when pressed about whether Brennan provided consultation or counsel during his tenure, but records just declassified by the White House reveal members of Smith's team met with Brennan while preparing the classified-documents case against President Donald Trump. The revelation about Brennan's meeting with special counsel Smith's team adds another wrinkle to Republicans' broader scrutiny of Smith's investigations into Trump, which has included claims of political bias, overreach and other investigative missteps. "Jack Smith was a tool of the Biden administration to put Trump in prison," said Harvard Law professor and former Trump impeachment counsel, Alan Dershowitz, who described Smith's work as "a partisan weapon that broke the rules, lied to the court and engaged in bad faith throughout" in a 2025 op-ed for The Wall Street Journal. Another critic, investigative reporter John Solomon, recently described the probes as among a "10-year conspiracy to stop Donald Trump using the resources of the United States government." EXPLOSIVE NEW REPORT PUTS JACK SMITH BACK IN HOT SEAT AS JIM JORDAN ALLEGES HE TRIED TO 'SWAY' 2024 ELECTION Two assistant special counsels working under Smith joined FBI agents for a November 2023 meeting with Brennan at CIA headquarters in McLean, Virginia, according to documents that were declassified Monday by the White House. The meeting was held "to discuss expert testimony to National Defense Information in the forthcoming trial," indicating prosecutors were exploring the possibility of using the former CIA chief's national security expertise as they prepared their case against Trump. Meanwhile, Smith appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee last week as part of the Republican-led panel's oversight of his investigations into Trump. During the hearing, GOP lawmakers pressed Smith over allegations of political bias, investigative overreach and misconduct in both the Arctic Frost 2020 election probe and his classified-documents case known as "Plasmic Echo." In particular, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, asked Smith whether he had ever received "consultation or counsel" from Brennan, including during his tenure as special counsel. EX-CIA CHIEF ACCUSED OF ORCHESTRATING 'RUSSIA HOAX' SUES TRUMP ADMIN FOR 'VINDICTIVE PROSECUTION' "Have you ever received any consultation or counsel by John Brennan, former CIA director, whether during your time as special counsel or otherwise? If so, when and for what purpose?" Grassley asked. "I've never met John Brennan," Smith responded. FORMER CIA DIRECTOR BRENNAN SUBPOENAED TO TESTIFY IN FEDERAL TRUMP CONSPIRACY CASE Grassley's question, however, was broader than whether Smith personally met Brennan, and the newly declassified records show prosecutors working directly under Smith met with the former CIA director as they prepared the government's case against Trump. "This meeting occurred during Jack Smith’s time as Special Counsel and constitutes ‘consultation or counsel’ from John Brennan to Smith and his team," Grassley told Fox News Digital. "Smith’s response before the Senate Judiciary Committee was highly evasive and misleading, at minimum." During the hearing, Grassley later returned to the issue, asking Smith whether he had ever had a conversation with Brennan. "I have no recollection of having a conversation with John Brennan," Smith responded. FBI QUESTIONING CURRENT AND FORMER CIA OFFICIALS IN DOJ PROBE INTO JOHN BRENNAN'S ROLE IN RUSSIA ASSESSMENT In addition to the memo outlining the 2023 Brennan meeting, the declassified release also included two pages of notes bearing CIA headquarters headers where lines of text beneath Brennan's name are blacked out by government redactions, leaving the remainder of the ruled pages blank. Brennan was not serving as CIA director during the period covered by Smith's classified-documents case, and the released records do not indicate he had firsthand knowledge of Trump's alleged handling of the documents. JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS Grassley, as well as other GOP lawmakers and critics, have accused the former special counsel of investigative overreach and political bias, including pointing to records showing his Arctic Frost investigation obtained financial information involving thousands of Trump donors and phone records of Republican lawmakers, among other investigative steps. Grassley has separately raised questions about the origins and conduct of Smith's classified-documents prosecution. Smith, meanwhile, has rejected allegations that his investigations were politically motivated and has maintained that his decisions were driven by the evidence and defending the work of prosecutors and investigators on his team. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to attorneys for Smith to obtain comment about the Brennan meeting, as well as the Justice Department, but did not receive a response.

articles.title: As concerns over health costs mount, Trump tries cash
articles.summary: With the midterm elections a month away and Republicans struggling to respond to voter frustration over healthcare costs, President Trump is handing out cash. Last week, Trump pledged $90 to more than tens of millions of seniors on Medicare. That announcement came on top of other pledges to send money to Americans, including $500 ObamaCare…
articles.body:
With the midterm elections a month away and Republicans struggling to respond to voter frustration over healthcare costs, President Trump is handing out cash.

Last week, Trump pledged $90 to more than tens of millions of seniors on Medicare. That announcement came on top of other pledges to send money to Americans, including $500 ObamaCare “refund” checks that the administration began sending to some Affordable Care Act (ACA) enrollees last week.

The president also reiterated a promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” to every adult U.S. citizen, contingent on Republicans retaining control of Congress.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The moves are a political Hail Mary that come as Republicans worry that the high cost of healthcare is one of the party’s greatest liabilities.

“I don’t think there’s any doubt Republicans have never been particularly good at healthcare messaging and I certainly don’t think we are winning the day on it right now,” said Jason Cabel Roe, a Michigan-based Republican strategist working on Rep. Tom Barrett’s (R-Mich.) campaign.

However, Cabel Roe said he hasn’t seen healthcare show up in polls as much as he thought it would.

“I think that’s probably leading people to maybe back off dedicating a lot of their messaging to healthcare,” he said.

But polling over the past year has consistently shown that voters are worried about the cost of healthcare — and trust Democrats more to fix it.

A survey this week from KFF found that healthcare costs and gas prices are tied as Americans’ top economic worries. Voters overall trust Democrats to handle healthcare costs by a nearly two-to-one margin over Republicans.

A Gallup survey from March found more Americans were concerned about the “availability and affordability of healthcare” more than any other domestic policy issue, and one-third made at least one tradeoff of daily living expenses to afford care.

And a KFF-AP poll from September showed even the GOP base was being hit hard by health cost pressures: By a more than a two-to-one margin, rural voters said the Trump administration’s policies have worsened their healthcare costs and access to care in their communities.

Democrats have historically had an advantage on healthcare, while voters have tended to trust Republicans more on economic issues.

“Part of the reason why Democrats are doing so well is because essentially they say things that sound good, but never actually work,” said Ford O’Connell, a GOP strategist and former Trump campaign surrogate.

Healthcare costs are a bridge issue, so it’s significant that Democrats have such an advantage.

“Healthcare costs are kind of at the intersection of both those as an economic and healthcare issue, and we’re seeing how Democrats are offering potentially some solutions to meet voters’ frustrations … whereas Republicans aren’t really talking about much other than fraud, waste, and abuse,” said Shannon Schumacher, a senior survey analyst for the Public Opinion and Survey Research program at KFF.

Mark Weaver, a GOP strategist in Ohio, said messaging over health costs is something that Republicans can overcome, but it’s a longer-term issue needing solutions that a Republican-majority Congress hasn’t delivered.

O’Connell said Republicans need to focus on saying “Medicare for All” would drive up costs and stress the current Medicare system, along with touting the work done by the GOP to bring down drug costs.

“You say, ‘Hey, here’s something we made affordable. Send us back to Washington and we will make sure aspects of our healthcare system more affordable for you,’” he said.

Trump has sought to shrug off affordability concerns, and the White House is framing Trump sending cash to millions of Americans as fulfilling his promise to lower costs.

“President Trump is delivering on his promises to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans,” the White House said in a statement about the Medicare payments.

More than 20 million Medicare Part B enrollees will receive $90, either by check or direct deposit. The standard Medicare Part B monthly premium is about $200.

The administration is also mailing out $500 “refund” checks for about 1 million people who the White House says were overcharged for Obamacare coverage.

“For years, the Biden administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov,” Trump wrote in a letter accompanying the checks. “That money belongs to hard-working Americans, not the Government, and now I’m returning it to you!”

But the checks will only go to enrollees who live in one of 30 states that use the federal government’s ACA exchange — many of them key battleground states — which leaves out about 18 million people.

Critics said the moves are a desperate gimmick that won’t even come close to repairing the damage the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have done to the health system.

Republicans are “in a world of hurt because they’ve put the American people into a world of hurt,” said Leslie Dach, founder and chair of the liberal health advocacy group Protect Our Care.

“People want assistance, but they see right through the gimmicks. What this administration is taking away from them is astronomical, and what they’re trying to give back is not going to solve their problems,” Dach said.

Weaver noted that it’s “a venerable tradition” for politicians to promise voters free money. Trump’s efforts “could help with the margins,” but it’s unclear if his message will energize anyone other than the base.

Cabel Roe said Trump’s messaging on healthcare is not very effective.

“Everything with him is impulse and not strategy so it’s not really helpful because no one knows what they should believe.”

articles.title: Trump heads to Texas as GOP worries mount over Paxton, Talarico
articles.summary: President Trump is headed back to Texas on Wednesday for his third visit in a month as Republican Ken Paxton trails Democrat James Talarico in a battleground Senate race. It’s the latest in Trump’s blitz through red states to rev up Republican voters as many key midterm forecasts shift in Democrats’ favor, and it’s his…
articles.body:
President Trump is headed back to Texas on Wednesday for his third visit in a month as Republican Ken Paxton trails Democrat James Talarico in a battleground Senate race.

It’s the latest in Trump’s blitz through red states to rev up Republican voters as many key midterm forecasts shift in Democrats’ favor, and it’s his latest move to put the national spotlight on the Lone Star State. He spoke at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) “Trump-a-palooza” rally in Dallas last month and rallied voters while visiting a motor plant in Denton last week.

Though Democrats have struggled for decades to win statewide in the red stronghold, Republicans are on defense amid Trump’s poor approval numbers and voter frustration with the economy, the war in Iran and immigration, as well as Paxton’s past controversies.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is expected to speak at the San Antonio rally , which he hopes will “keep Texas red and keep America first,” as is Republican House hopeful Carlos De La Cruz, who’s locked in a tight race against Democrat Johnny Garcia in the 35th District.

“Republicans are worried. They need Trump to elevate Republican turnout, and it’s clear that Paxton on his own can’t do it,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston.

“We’re not used to seeing this many visits from our president, and I think that the upshot is that it’s a real warning sign for Republicans.”

Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) latest polling averages show Talarico roughly 3 percentage points ahead of Paxton, based on recent surveys showing a race that’s within the margins of error . Vote Hub on Monday moved the race from a “tilt D” rating to an even more favorable “lean D” label for Democrats.

Cook Political Report shifted the Talarico-Paxton race away from Republicans to a “toss-up” rating in August. DDHQ also considers it a coin flip but narrowly favors Democrats, giving Talarico a 56 percent probability of flipping the seat.

The close numbers have already made it the most expensive Senate race of the cycle — but with Paxton still trailing as Election Day nears, more funds are flooding in on both sides of the aisle.

President Trump’s MAGA Inc. dropped $10 million into the race in early September. Tech mogul Elon Musk’s super PAC has spent more than $6 million for Paxton in recent weeks, according to the San Antonio Current. And Texas PAC, affiliated with the GOP Senate Leadership Fund, spent a whopping $131 million for Paxton, per Axios.

On the Democratic side, top groups aren’t yet spending big in the state, but the party’s Senate campaign super PAC was preparing last week to make an initial investment in the Texas race for the upper chamber. And Talarico has brought in big hauls, with a staggering $30 million raised in the second quarter against Paxton’s $9 million that period.

Paxton brought in $18 million in the third quarter of the year, his campaign shared Monday, and Talarico has yet to release his third-quarter numbers.

“This is a very close and super tight race. So the smallest things are going to make a difference,” Texas GOP consultant Vinny Minchillo said.

“This is a turnout election, and has been from the very beginning. And bringing the president in is going to rally the faithful — that’s the plan — and to make sure that people get out and turn out for the whole Republican ticket, and certainly for Ken Paxton.”

Last month, Trump used the RNC’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas as a platform to boost Paxton on his home turf. Trump quipped to the convention crowd that he doesn’t “like the way Ken dresses,” “talks” or “looks,” but he argued the Republican is “the greatest” attorney general in the country.

Paxton, however, has struggled to catch up to Talarico — and he said as much in leaked audio shared by The New York Times last week.

“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good,” Paxton said in the clip, though a Paxton adviser later called The Times reporting “manipulated nonsense.”

In his Denton stop last week, Trump quipped that Paxton was “a pain in the a‑‑” and “a little controversial.”

“I think that’s a colorful way to say, ‘Hey, the guy’s got baggage,’ which is no secret … but you know, ‘He’s our guy and you need to support him,’” Minchillo said of the president’s Paxton pitch.

Paxton, who defeated incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) for the party nod with the help of Trump’s eleventh-hour endorsement, was a controversial Senate pick for the party. As the state’s top attorney, he faced criticism of politicizing the office and weathered an unsuccessful 2023 impeachment on corruption charges. His wife of nearly four decades filed for divorce last year on “biblical grounds.”

But Trump, too, is unpopular — making his red-state stops a “catch-22” for Republican candidates, Rottinghaus said.

“Obviously, he’s supported among core Republicans who the GOP needs to turn out, but he’s also toxic among many in the Democratic field and among swing voters. So there’s a kind of trade-off there for Republicans when it comes down to it,” Rottinghaus said of Trump.

And the Senate race isn’t the only marquee fight in Texas.

Gov. Greg Abbott (R) is not expected to attend the rally due to scheduling conflicts as he battles Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has made her own gains in recent polls of the red-leaning race.

Trump is also using the San Antonio rally to support De La Cruz, the brother of Texas Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R), in an open race against Garcia for a seat reshaped by GOP-friendly redistricting. It’s one of four Texas House contests that Cook Political Report considers highly competitive.

But Republicans may ultimately gain nothing at the national level from redistricting, according to a recent DDHQ analysis — and though they hoped to win five more seats in Texas, experts say they may snag only two or three.

That’s driven in part by a shift among Latino voters, who represent roughly a third of the state’s eligible voters. The bloc turned to Trump in 2024 but now appears increasingly frustrated with the president’s handling of the economy and immigration.

“Democrats are in the best position they’ve been in for at least a decade,” Rottinghaus said of the Lone Star State landscape. “And they need to take advantage of this.”

articles.title: What a post-midterm House Freedom Caucus could look like
articles.summary: The House Freedom Caucus is heading into 2027 with a leadership shake-up and a new opportunity to shape how the influential conservative bloc operates, as several of its most prominent figures prepare to leave Congress. The caucus’s current policy chair, Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), and a number of other influential members, including GOP Reps. Ralph…
articles.body:
The House Freedom Caucus is heading into 2027 with a leadership shake-up and a new opportunity to shape how the influential conservative bloc operates, as several of its most prominent figures prepare to leave Congress.

The caucus’s current policy chair, Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), and a number of other influential members, including GOP Reps. Ralph Norman (S.C.), Andy Biggs (Ariz.), Byron Donalds (Fla.), Tom Tiffany (Wis.) and Barry Moore (Ala.), are leaving the House.

Their exit raises big questions about how the Freedom Caucus will operate — and how much influence it will wield — in the next Congress.

To be sure, if Democrats win control of the House, the caucus — along with all Republicans — will lose a great deal of power.

With the GOP in charge of a narrowly divided chamber, the Freedom Caucus has leverage as Republican leaders have needed to win their support before big votes. Democrats are not going to come calling.

Even so, President Trump will still control the White House, and Freedom Caucus members say they have no plans to ease up on their priorities — or their own leadership when it comes to fighting for conservative policies. Several pledge to push even harder to advance the caucus’s agenda and push GOP leaders to resist bipartisan deals that fall short of that goal.

Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) told The Hill that he expects everyone in the Republican conference to be a “flaming conservative” if the party loses the House majority.

“I will tell you, we will continue to do what we’ve done in the Congress’s past,” Self said, referring to how the caucus has pushed for a ban on central bank digital currency, Second Amendment protections, codifying Trump’s border policies and pushing the Senate to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

Self, along with fellow GOP Reps. Eric Burlison (Mo.) and Clay Higgins (La.), are considered rising leaders in the caucus, according to a person familiar with its dynamics. Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) is another big voice in the caucus who has been seen as playing an active role in promoting conservative policies.

The Freedom Caucus was often a pest to GOP leaders, but it was an effective one that extracted concessions from Republican leaders on critical votes.

Earlier this year, Roy, Self, Burlison, Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) and other members voted against a procedural rule that would have teed up major defense and funding legislation. The members were frustrated over the lack of action on a border bill and the SAVE America Act.

“Whoever is in leadership, we are going to continue a continuous conversation with [them] early and often to make sure that the Freedom Caucus ideas and positions are well known early,” Self said.

“I think that’s a real key, is to make sure that everybody understands where we are, so that can be factored into the leadership calculus. So yeah, we’re going to continue to be very vocal and engaged with the leadership and the White House as we go forward to make sure that our positions are well understood and vocalized.”

Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.) said that “when the Republicans are in the minority, everybody is a member of the Freedom Caucus.”

He also suggested the caucus could have tremendous influence in this year’s lame-duck agenda, including by preventing the movement of any omnibus spending package.

Congress had passed a stopgap measure that would temporarily fund the government through Dec. 11. Both chambers must pass spending legislation to prevent a government shutdown at the end of the year.

“We’re getting close to Christmas, and we want to make sure that there’s not some sort of massive Christmas omnibus, all right, that sort of thing,” Clyde said.

One of the most immediate tasks for the caucus after the midterm elections will be determining who is the new chair. The caucus’s current chair, Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.), will have to step down from his role as he is term-limited.

“We’ve got some good young members that I think are going to want to step up, so I’m going to wait and see,” said Self of the possibility he could run for chair. He said he is “not prepared to commit to that.”

Another priority will be bringing new members up to speed on the ways of Congress and teaching them how to navigate the institution effectively, several members said.

The Freedom Caucus Fund, the PAC affiliated with the caucus, has endorsed several GOP candidates, including David Flippo, a Trump-endorsed Air Force veteran running in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, and Brandon Herrera, a gun rights YouTuber running in Texas’s 23rd Congressional District.

“I think we are very well positioned. We’ve got a very strong board of directors with tremendous experience. I’m on the board. I’m one of those, I think, and I think the future is very bright with the Freedom Caucus. I think one of our, well, actually, the whole focus of the Freedom Caucus is to move the Republican Conference to the right… to be as conservative as 218 votes will allow,” Clyde said.

Fine did not consider the possibility that Republicans could lose the majority.

“I’m going to assume that we’re going to keep the majority, and I think our role is to be pushing the party to the right, you know, to be dealing with the thorny problems that sometimes get pushed aside because people focus on political considerations,” the Florida congressman told The Hill.

“So, for example, our country is going to collapse in the lifetime of our children if we don’t deal with the debt and the deficit, the thorny issues of legal immigration that is destroying the complexion of our country, what it means to be an American, and our values. I mean, these are real issues that need to be tackled, and people like to say, ‘After the next election, after the next election.’ Well, it’s about to be after the next election, and it’s going to be time to deal with some of these problems,” Fine added.

articles.title: GOP senators warn that Trump has fumbled immigration issue
articles.summary: Republican senators say President Trump has fumbled the issue of immigration, something that was an advantage for GOP candidates in 2024 but is now a growing political liability for their party. Several GOP senators told The Hill that Trump’s deportation policy has gone too far and warn that it’s hurting Republican candidates with suburban and…
articles.body:
Republican senators say President Trump has fumbled the issue of immigration, something that was an advantage for GOP candidates in 2024 but is now a growing political liability for their party.

Several GOP senators told The Hill that Trump’s deportation policy has gone too far and warn that it’s hurting Republican candidates with suburban and Hispanic voters.

These GOP critics say Trump’s mass-deportation policies have been too aggressive and are eclipsing his big policy wins, such as reducing illegal border crossings by more than 90 percent since former President Biden left office.

“Once you start deporting people who have otherwise been here without incident for 15, 20 years, that’s a gray zone that I think where you find a lot of division of opinion,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

“I always thought that this idea of mass deportations sent the wrong message,” he added.

A nationwide Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted from Sept. 11-14 found that 53 percent of voters thought the Trump administration’s enforcement of immigration laws had gone too far.

Of those who said deportations had gone too far, 45 percent said the government was using too much force, while 49 percent said the wrong people were being targeted.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who’s running for reelection this year, said most Americans want Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to target migrants who have committed crimes other than crossing the border illegally.

“Most Americans are saying we are a nation of laws, but with as many people here illegally as we’ve got, let’s make darn sure that our focus is on getting those individuals that have violated our laws with regard to other things other than being here illegally,” he said.

Rounds advised the Trump administration to ease off on immigrants who “are here and that have a court determination that [says] they can be here.”

He suggested “we not go after them” and instead “refocus on those individuals that are actually causing harm within society today.”

“Most Americans will tell you that just in terms of their sense of fairness, they would prefer to go after individuals who have been violating our [criminal] laws,” he said.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said he agrees with his Senate GOP colleagues that Trump’s mass deportations have gone too far.

“I would rather have 100 illegally present people go free than have that innocent person caught,” he said. “They’re right.”

“If you’re going to put somebody through that, you better be damn sure you have a justified basis for doing it,” he said of immigration enforcement sweeps that have caught up citizens and green-card holders.

An investigation by ProPublica found that more than 170 U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents, including some Americans who have been tackled, beaten and shocked with Tasers by federal immigration enforcement officers.

“Aside from it being politically dumb, it’s immoral, in my opinion,” Tillis said.

Tillis said Trump’s overreach on mass deportations has eclipsed his significant accomplishments on border security.

“Instead of taking that win … we’ve completely masked that enormous success of securing the border, by overreaching and going too aggressively” after mass deportations, he argued.

The Hill reached out to the White House and the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll of 1,280 registered voters nationwide conducted from Sept. 14-15 found that 41 percent of voters thought Democrats would do a better job than Republicans on the issue of immigration.

The survey found 38 percent of voters thought Republicans would do a better job on the issue.

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), who is retiring but represents another Senate battleground state, said people who enter the country illegally broke the law. At the same time, she asked if there is a “more humane way” to address residents who have lived here illegally for a long time.

“It’s hard because, again, they are here illegally but at the same time if they have been contributing members [of society], what is a way that we perhaps could work with the situation and capitalize on it? Is there a way that President Trump could look at these individuals and say, ‘OK, we’ll allow you to stay but we’re going to tax you more … as a way of paying a fine because you broke the law entering the country,’” she said.

GOP lawmakers said public opinion began to shift significantly on Trump’s immigration policies after two American citizens were shot and killed by federal officers in Minneapolis during street demonstrations protesting ICE’s and Border Patrol’s aggressive tactics.

The fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37, sparked a public backlash and triggered a 76-day shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) after Democrats blocked its appropriations bill.

The DHS was eventually funded in a separate bill that was approved through a budget reconciliation process. Under those budgetary rules, the bill could not be filibustered, and the DHS funding, through the Trump administration, was approved only on GOP votes in the Senate.

Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that supports restricting immigration numbers, pushed back against the Republican criticism.

He argued that Trump took steps to address public concerns after the high-profile shootings in Minneapolis.

“They’re doing the job in a more professional and less cinematic fashion,” he said of immigration enforcement officials. “The complaints now you’re hearing about the current approach to immigration enforcement are coming from Republicans who never supported the president’s agenda to begin with, including Cornyn.”

Still, Republican senators are growing increasingly alarmed that Trump’s handling of immigration is shifting Hispanic voters toward Democrats in key races.

An NBC News/Telemundo poll of 800 Hispanic voters conducted from Sept. 21-28 found that only 27 percent of them approved of Trump, while 69 percent disapproved.

The survey revealed 7 in 10 Hispanic voters disapproved of Trump’s handling of immigration and that 20 percent of Hispanic voters who backed Trump in 2024 now said they do not prefer a GOP-controlled Congress.

Cornyn, who represents a state with a large Hispanic population, pointed to a recent ad by Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) criticizing Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts for having “gone too far.”

“She’s saying what a lot of Hispanics have been thinking, which [is] very aggressive enforcement against people who aren’t criminals, who aren’t a threat to public safety — among Hispanics, particularly — there’s a sense it’s gone too far,” he said.

“Among Hispanics, in the polling I’ve seen [it] indicates that that is a problem,” he added.

Cornyn said the Hispanic vote could be decisive in determining the outcome of the Texas Senate race between state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and state Rep. James Talarico (D). Polls have shown Talarico with a lead in the race, which the Cook Political Report lists as a toss-up contest.

Republicans are defending a Senate majority where the map continues to get wider. Cook on Tuesday moved the Kansas Senate race to toss-up, and the race to succeed Tillis in North Carolina as likely Democrat.

Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.), who hails from one of the most pro-Trump states in the country, last week told Politico that the Trump administration should reconsider its aggressive immigration enforcement policies.

“Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years, and I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” Justice told the publication.

The popular former West Virginia governor, however, backtracked after his comment gained widespread attention.

“Let me be crystal clear: I support President Trump’s immigration strategy, full stop. It’s not surprising that some are twisting my words to score political points, but there should be no confusion about where I stand,” Justice later explained in a post on the social platform X.

articles.title: Unearthed clip exposes stunning Talarico claim about 'students of color’ in Texas public schools
articles.summary: James Talarico criticized Texas public schools for focusing too heavily on academics, arguing social-emotional learning matters more than the curriculum.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico once criticized the Texas public school system for focusing too heavily on academics while arguing that social-emotional learning should receive greater attention and also declared that Texas schools were "not built" for "poor students" or "students of color." "I was trapped in a system that was focused purely on academics, reading, writing, arithmetic. And there wasn't time to talk about social-emotional learning," Talarico said in a 2020 discussion with Texas Rising — a progressive youth activist group. "All the things that we all know on this call are more important than whether or not you memorize the quadratic equation," he continued. 'FAKE' MODERATE TALARICO'S TEXAS SURGE TESTS PAXTON IN FIGHT TO HOLD CRUCIAL GOP SENATE SEAT Talarico made the comments while serving in the Texas House of Representatives, representing the 52nd District, after working as a public school teacher for just two years. His time working in education became a central point in his work in the legislature and now in his Senate campaign. In the unearthed discussion, Talarico said that he felt like he wasn’t able to have "the really important conversations" with his students that "would allow them to live a fulfilling life." He said that he was, instead, forced to focus on teaching the school curriculum rather than "social-emotional" lessons. He also used the discussion to slam the Texas public school system as "not built" for "poor students" and "students of color." "Our public education system, particularly here in Texas, is not built for poor students," Talarico said. "It's not built for students of color." UNEARTHED CLIP SHOWS TALARICO CALLING PARENTS 'ABUSIVE' FOR DENYING CHILDREN'S GENDER IDENTITY Talarico claimed this motivated him to introduce his "Whole Student Agenda" in 2019 — a series of 24 bills which pushed for a variety of reforms including modifications for "scientifically accurate" sex education and encouraging restorative justice programs. Despite Talarico saying the system is "not built for students of color," the package does not specifically address race-related issues. The Texas Democrat has repeatedly been under fire for his progressive education work in the legislature, particularly his push for sexual education, DEI policies, law enforcement reforms and climate conversations. Talarico described sex education as "maybe the most important topic" for Texas students to learn during a Texas House hearing in 2022. He also characterized bills addressing concerns about inappropriate school materials as "conspiracy theory-driven" and "kooky stuff." TALARICO CAMPAIGNS WITH SURGEON WHO OPERATED ON TRANSGENDER MINORS: ‘WOLF IN SHEEP’S CLOTHING’ He led a bill in the Texas House requiring most Texas school districts to hire a diversity, equity and inclusion officer, as well as for DEI to "explicitly" be taught in every classroom in the public school system. Talarico has also faced scrutiny over his education consulting work while serving on the Texas House Public Education Committee. Fox News Digital previously reported that a firm employing Talarico received millions of dollars in contracts from the Texas Education Agency while he served on the committee. His campaign denied wrongdoing, calling the allegation a "lie." Talarico will go head-to-head with GOP Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton in the upcoming midterm elections, a race expected to be crucial in determining which party will take control of the Senate. articles.title: Florida poll: Republicans lead in the races for governor and Senate
articles.summary: The new survey shows the state’s Hispanic voters shifting away from President Donald Trump after Republicans made gains in 2024.
articles.body: Republican Byron Donalds holds a 7-percentage-point advantage over Democrat David Jolly in the Florida governor’s race, according to a new NBC South Florida/Telemundo Station Group poll, while Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is up by 10 points in her matchup against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon. Donalds, a congressman from the southwest corner of the state, is at 48% in the poll, compared with Jolly’s 41%, in a race in which Donalds has had a commanding financial advantage. (That advantage is just inside the poll’s margin of error, but Donalds has the edge in most of the range of possibilities.) Moody is at 50% in the Senate race, compared with 40% for Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who got into the general election after a surprise primary victory over Democrat Alexander Vindman in August. The results come amid broad Democratic optimism about the 2026 elections, with public polling showing the party making races in some typically red states into competitive contests this year. This poll suggests limits to that apparent momentum in other places. The poll also took a snapshot of the state’s hugely influential bloc of Hispanic voters, largely congregated in South Florida. In 2024, Donald Trump won Hispanic-heavy Miami-Dade County by roughly 11 points, a significant reversal in a part of the state that had long been Democratic-leaning. Joe Biden won the county by 7 points in 2020. But now, Florida Hispanic voters — including large Cuban, Nicaraguan, Honduran and Colombian populations — appear to be swinging back away from Trump, even as other high-profile Republican candidates hold comfortable leads among Hispanic voters. Donalds holds a 48%-43% lead over Jolly among Hispanic voters, according to the survey, while Moody is up 47%-40% over Nixon. Trump’s job performance rating, however, is underwater, with 49% disapproving of his job performance, compared with 45% who approve. Overall, 48% of all Florida likely voters approve of Trump’s job performance and 48% disapprove. Before Trump’s gains among Florida’s Hispanic population in 2024, Democrats had generally won the demographic in the state by comfortable margins. Democrats argue that recent special election victories in Florida show the party has already started winning back the Hispanic vote, in part because of Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy. Unhappiness with prices and the cost of living has also affected Trump’s ratings among Hispanic voters. “In legislative races in Florida, we have seen huge swings,” Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NBC News last week, speaking of the committee’s efforts in Florida House races. She said that on immigration, Trump and his party broke a promise “to go after the worst of the worst.” By far the most important issue identified was inflation and the cost of living, with 30% saying it is likeliest to influence their votes. In both the overall sample and the sample of Hispanic voters, “direction of the state or country” (17%) was the second most important issue. The broader polling data put “immigration enforcement” as the third most important issue (16%), while the Hispanic sample put property taxes (13%) as the third most important issue. Immigration enforcement was the fourth most important issue among Hispanic voters (12%). Questions about the Trump administration’s push to allow local and state policy to cooperate with federal immigration officials fell along party lines. Among all voters, 85% of Republicans support the policy, compared with 18% of Democrats and 44% of those identified as independent voters who supported the harsher immigration enforcement tactics. Property taxes have also been front and center in Florida during the midterms. The state Republican Party and term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis support a ballot measure, known as Amendment 3, that would increase property tax exemptions to the first $250,000 of a home’s value by 2028. The exemption cap is currently $50,000. In the poll of all Florida voters, 55% back the amendment, 26% oppose it, and 19% are undecided. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of Republicans supported the idea, compared with 36% for Democrats and 43% for independents. The overall survey questioned 625 registered voters, all of whom said they were likely to vote in the November elections. They were interviewed over the telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research Inc. from Sept. 28 to Thursday, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The same time frame and methods were used to survey 400 Hispanic registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.

articles.title: Americans spend most on groceries in these 15 cities, study finds
articles.summary: Inflation has backed off from the eye-watering double digit numbers after the pandemic, but unfortunately for Americans grocery store prices haven’t gone down – an especially painful trend for residents of some U.S. cities, according to a new study.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Inflation has backed off from the eye-watering double digit numbers after the pandemic, but unfortunately for Americans, grocery store prices haven’t gone down – an especially painful trend for residents of some U.S. cities, according to a new study.

As the cost of a week’s worth of food ticks higher across the country , residents who spend the largest share of their income on groceries also tend to have lower incomes, making them especially vulnerable to rising prices, according to personal finance site WalletHub .

Americans spent an average of 12.9% of their pretax incomes on eating out and at home in 2024, but the share was 33% for the one-fifth of U.S. households with the lowest earnings, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Prices also can vary substantially by region. In St. Louis, food for home use cost 2% more in June compared to a year earlier; in San Francisco, it was 6%, the consumer price index showed.

The WalletHub study, published Wednesday, ranks the top 100 largest cities by the percentage of income residents spend on groceries annually, on average, with Detroit in the top spot.

Groceries in the Motor City take up 4.03% of household income on average, the highest in the nation. While the cost of food is somewhat comparable, with staples like beef, tuna and peaches cheaper than in most stores in the country, Detroit has the lowest median annual household income ($39,938). Nearly a third of residents (32.7%) live below the federal poverty level, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

“As a result, every dollar that people in Detroit spend on groceries takes up a disproportionately high share of their earnings compared to people in cities with higher incomes,” according to the study.

Despite its cheap whole milk, coffee and peaches, Cleveland ranked second (3.93%) because it also has the second-lowest median household income ($40,801), according to the latest government statistics .

With the average cost of a pound of ground beef nearing $7 – it was under $3.80 in 2019 – many Americans may be wondering how we got here, and what they can do to spend less.

The historic increase happened for numerous reasons. The coronavirus pandemic snarled supply chains and raised labor and transportation costs. Droughts, hurricanes and diseases like bird flu drove down production. Tariffs raised prices on foreign products like coffee, tomatoes and chocolate. Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine disrupted oil and fertilizer supplies.

With a fresh conflict in the Middle East accelerating food price inflation again this year, the cost of filling their refrigerators, freezers and pantries has become a frustration for Americans and made affordability a central issue in the fall midterm elections.

“I think the public is coming to grips with, ‘Well, I’m hearing inflation has slowed, but things aren’t getting any cheaper.’ It has to be deflation for prices to go down, and that’s very rare,” said Matt Hamory, who leads the global grocery practice at the consulting company AlixPartners.

Groceries are an unavoidable monthly cost for most Americans – so what can people do to lessen inflation’s impact on their bank accounts?

“Shoppers should take advantage of sales and coupons, buy generic items and buy in bulk if possible in order to save money,” Wallethub writer and analyst Chip Lupo recommends. “It’s also a good idea to use a credit card that gives a good amount of rewards on grocery purchases and pay it off in full each month.”

Experts say there is already evidence that shoppers are changing their habits, with discounters like Costco, Walmart and Aldi gaining market share from some of the country’s major grocery stores like Kroger and Albertsons.

Shoppers are also embracing store brands at supermarkets, drugstores and other retailers, with last year’s sales reaching a record $282.8 billion, according to the Private Label Manufacturers Association.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
