articles.title: Sen. Ruben Gallego rolls out an economic agenda as he weighs a 2028 White House bid
articles.summary: The Arizona Democrat told NBC News he’s “absolutely thinking about” running for president. He’s pitching a New Deal-style jobs program funded by data center and AI taxes.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who is eyeing a possible presidential bid in 2028, rolled out a new, national economic plan Wednesday that calls for boosting the minimum wage to $20 per hour and a New Deal-style public service jobs program funded by taxes on artificial intelligence companies and unpopular data centers. In an interview with NBC News, Gallego said middle-class and working-class Americans are under assault due to rapidly advancing artificial intelligence and automation, as well as an economic system that has not sided with nor supported workers for a generation. “There’s a lot of changes that are coming because of AI that we’re not prepared for. There’s been a lot of bad things that have been happening for the middle class for the last 40 years that we have not really changed, either. And that’s why I think you have this real anxiety out there that working America feels,” Gallego said in an interview Tuesday. “I always felt like, you know, if I put 40 hours’ worth of honest work together, I would have enough to support my family, and then feel comfortable enough to go to a movie,” he continued. “That’s not happening anymore, and so that’s the most important focus of this plan.” The November midterm elections are still weeks away, with both the House and Senate up for grabs, but Gallego’s decision to launch his AI and economic agenda now underscores just how quickly the political conversation will shift to what’s expected to be a crowded Democratic presidential contest. Asked whether he plans to run in 2028, Gallego said he is considering it and trying to determine whether he can balance a grueling presidential bid with raising three young children. “I’m not, you know, going to lie and say we’re not thinking about it. We are absolutely thinking about it,” said the 46-year-old senator, who was raised by a single mother and frequently talks about his up-from-the-bootstraps personal narrative. He has “a young family,” he said, “so that has to be the most important thing. How do you balance running for that office, mind you, and, you know, still be an active father? That’s very difficult to do, and I have to have a family, you know, fully into that.” But regardless of that decision, he emphasized that Democrats need to state what they stand for. “We want to make sure that people understand what I believe we should be focusing on starting in 2027 and going all the way through, whether I run for president or not,” he said. Gallego’s detailed, 32-page plan, dubbed “Saving the Middle Class and Restoring the American Dream,” is a mix of dozens of populist ideas and pragmatic proposals. He divides it into five pillars: “Raise Wages and Improve Benefits,” “Create and Protect Quality Blue-Collar Jobs,” “Restore Worker Trust in Government in the Age of Artificial Intelligence,” “Expand Job-Creating Entrepreneurship, Focusing Outside of Superstar Cities,” and “Help Workers Find Jobs Faster.” Amid recent warnings that AI could soon cause human extinction, Gallego’s proposals on AI and data centers are perhaps the timeliest. He wants to establish a Franklin D. Roosevelt-style public service jobs program — funded by taxes on data centers and an excise tax on revenue from large AI companies — that would pay for jobs that “promote human connection and community cohesion.” Those could include coaching Little League; counseling people fighting addiction; beautifying neighborhoods; and caring for children, older adults, or sick or disabled people, according to the plan. “My son’s Little League in Phoenix sometimes does not have enough coaches, does not have enough referees. There are leagues of that nature all around the country that we could be working with them to fully fund coaching programs, mentoring programs, childcare,” Gallego said. “We could pay people if they want to stay at home with their kids.” Gallego is also proposing allowing individuals to charge tech companies for using their personal data; imposing a “robot” tax to discourage corporations from shifting jobs away from humans; and requiring companies to have humans review AI or automated workplace decisions, including hiring or laying off employees. “Making sure that human bodies are more valuable to the workspace than robotic bodies,” he said, “because right now, the way that our tax policies are actually tilted, it’s actually tilted more for automation than for actually human people working in a workplace.” Other ideas include tripling “union density,” or the percentage of workers in a particular industry in a union, by 2035; promoting “sectoral bargaining” to establish minimum labor standards across an entire industry; and requiring companies to pay double for overtime work rather than time and a half. While many of his policy prescriptions are critical of President Donald Trump and his administration, Gallego also takes aim at his own party. At the conclusion of his proposal, he declares: “This bipartisan, failed status quo must end.” Speaking to NBC News, Gallego said both parties share blame for the nation’s current problems. “I’m not saying that Democrats are worse than Republicans. I think on par, if you look at it, who has been worse for the working class in this country? It’s been Republicans, but Democrats can’t not be blamed in this,” he said. “Corporations made massive amounts of money, shareholders made massive amounts of money, but the persons that basically started it all just got thrown to the side, right?” he continued. “And there should have been stronger negotiations led by Democrats during NAFTA and during all these trade deals that said, ‘You know what, we’ll have trade, but that wealth is going to be shared back down with the people that actually made us wealthy in the first place, these workers.’ We never went down that road.” If he does mount a bid for president, Gallego’s past friendship with former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., who resigned this year amid sexual assault allegations, could become a liability. Swalwell denied any sexual misconduct, and Gallego said he was not aware of inappropriate behavior by his then-friend. Asked if that will be a distraction going forward, Gallego said the issue has already been heavily scrutinized. “I think we’ve been extremely scrutinized ... by the press. They’ve turned over every leaf and every aspect of my life. You know, they had an Ethics Committee that also looked into it, and everything’s come out, you know, clean,” Gallego said. The Senate Ethics Committee dismissed a complaint against Gallego, brought by Republican Rep. Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, saying it found no evidence of inappropriate sexual conduct or a campaign finance violation. “We’ve been focusing on good work and campaigning all across the country for Democrats. ... People have seen the value that I bring to the Democratic Party. ... And as long as I continue to really lean in with forward-leaning policies that are really calling to what America needs right now,” he said, “that’s going to be the biggest determination of my future.”

articles.title: America cannot win the global AI race if Americans are afraid to use AI
articles.summary: After Trump's White House AI accord, an EqualAI survey shows 46% of Americans distrust AI with their data, but 63% want independent scientific review.
articles.body: The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and xAI recently joined President Trump at the White House to sign a voluntary accord on artificial intelligence. Its commitments are concrete: stronger internal controls, independent outside evaluation and board-level review. The harder question, which remains to be seen, is whether it will earn the confidence of the people expected to live and work with these systems, who have been increasingly resistant to AI proliferation. America cannot win the AI race if Americans are afraid to use AI. AI ISN’T JUST A PROBLEM, IT’S A SOLUTION. SOME PEOPLE ARE ALREADY MAKING THE MOST OF IT I often say that one of the biggest challenges we have to fear about AI is the fear of AI itself. That fear is becoming a national liability. In a new EqualAI survey conducted by YouGov, 46% of Americans said they would be uncomfortable with a company using AI in a way that involves them or their data, regardless of safeguards. Yet 71% said a positive experience with an AI system would increase their confidence in it, and 63% said the same of a positive evaluation by independent scientists. That 63% is an important window into mechanisms to trust — and offers a bridge to build it. People do not want assurances; they want verification. AI will deliver for our economy, national security and competitiveness in the ways we are envisioning only if Americans actually use it. A nurse who does not trust an AI-enabled diagnostic tool will not rely on it. A manufacturer that cannot understand what its AI agents are doing will not deploy them at scale. AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK That is why we need to be thoughtful when discussing "pause," because if it does not include capable competitors, such as Chinese companies, the technology continues to advance but elsewhere and without the guardrails we’d like to establish. The question we need to answer is: what will make Americans confident enough to adopt AI? The debate is too often framed as more rules versus fewer rules. A more useful dialogue centers on how we can build the governance capacity to let AI scale. The public is telling us we have work to do. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 73% of Americans believe AI companies have not done enough to prevent serious harm from their technology; 55% said they would support slowing AI development. The EqualAI polling points to what could change that equation: 63% want independent scientific review of AI systems, while 60% support third-party audits. Sixty-eight percent say it is essential to be able to correct wrong information, and 65% say the ability to appeal an AI-driven decision is essential. When I testified before the House Select Committee, I heard strong, bipartisan interest in getting this right. My message was straightforward: American leadership on AI requires leadership in AI governance. Congress can use authorities it already has, including procurement, agency governance and consumer protection, as well as clarifying AI-specific protections, such as establishing definitions and protocols for AI incident reporting, as they’ve done for cyber incidents, and defining accountability for AI use cases with higher risk levels and making AI literacy a national competitiveness priority. And companies don't need to wait for Washington. Every leadership team deploying AI should ensure they’ve taken these four steps: First, make AI visible. You cannot govern what you cannot see. Organizations should know the who, what, where, when and how: where AI is deployed, what it can do and access, who owns it, when it will be tested and how unexpected outcomes will be addressed. WHEN AI TESTS CAUSE DAMAGE, WE NEED STRONGER SAFEGUARDS AND REAL ACCOUNTABILITY Second, establish independent evaluation. The institutional model is open to debate. The underlying questions are not: Who evaluates AI systems? Against what benchmarks? And what happens when a system fails? Third, create a system to identify and handle significant AI incidents. Define incidents and ensure all responsible parties understand escalation pathways and reporting obligations. We also need the federal government to establish these. Fourth, require accountability. Every organization should have a point person for deployments in certain risk categories. As AI becomes more agentic, systems can take actions rather than simply generate information. Responsible officers should ensure an agent only has the minimum access required. Finally, ensure your workforce and families are AI literate. People do not need to become engineers. They need to understand what AI can and cannot do, when to question it and when human judgment must remain in charge. We have navigated technological inflection points before. Cars did not become less innovative when we established licenses, traffic lights and global safety standards. Those institutions made mass adoption possible. AI will be no different. Governance accelerates trust and, as a result, adoption. The answer is not to slow technological progress until we eliminate every risk. Nor is it to tell Americans to trust AI just because we want them to. As we accelerate AI development and capabilities, we need to match pace with the mechanisms that enable our capacity to govern it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP America's advantage has never been simply building powerful technologies. It is that we build along with the institutions and standards that allow powerful technologies to be trusted and adopted at scale. This moment asks us to do that again.

articles.title: Trump’s onslaught tests Talarico’s momentum in Texas
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Debate night in key races ▪ Backlash to Trump’s California comment ▪ Cornell faculty raise no-confidence vote ▪ Israel marks Oct. 7 anniversary President Trump is returning to Texas today for the third time in less than a month, as Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico maintains his edge in the race…
articles.body:
▪ Backlash to Trump’s California comment

▪ Cornell faculty raise no-confidence vote

President Trump is returning to Texas today for the third time in less than a month, as Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico maintains his edge in the race despite an onslaught of GOP spending, including from Trump’s own war chest.

Trump will rally at 7 p.m. EDT in San Antonio for Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton (R) and congressional candidate Carlos De La Cruz (R), who is running in the newly redrawn 35th Congressional District.

Trump carried the state by 14 points in 2024, his biggest margin in Texas across his three presidential runs, but his return to the Lone Star State — less than a week after visiting a truck manufacturing plant in Denton, Texas — underscores the GOP’s vulnerability heading into the midterm elections.

San Antonio is home to two of the most competitive districts in the state: the 35th Congressional District and the 23rd Congressional District, which former moderate GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales represented before resigning earlier this year. In both districts, according to The Texas Tribune , most eligible voters are Hispanic.

Trump’s 2024 gains in Texas were largely driven by an uptick in support from Hispanic voters. But early October polling from The New York Times/Siena University shows Hispanic voters now favoring Talarico 62 percent to 30 percent over Paxton. That 32-point advantage is larger than Talarico’s 16-point lead among women, and close to his 36-point lead among adults under 30.

Overall, among all likely voters surveyed, Talarico now leads Paxton by 6 points, 51 percent to 45 percent, with 4 percent undecided. In the June Times/Siena poll, the candidates were tied at 47 percent.

The recent poll comes as Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ ), The Hill’s partner, gives Talarico a 56 percent chance of winning the seat, a forecast that has remained relatively stable for more than a month. The candidates’ chances both hovered around 50 percent throughout the month of August.

Democrats are wary of getting their hopes up again in a state that has only gotten redder since Beto O’Rourke came within striking distance of a Senate win in 2018. To defeat Paxton, Talarico would need strong Democratic turnout, majority support from independent voters and even some crossover votes from Republicans.

But Talarico’s polling numbers are stronger than O’Rourke’s ever were in another midterm election year two years after Trump took office. Democrats last won a Senate seat in Texas in 1988 and have not won a statewide race since 1994.

Along with Trump’s three trips to Texas and the GOP’s decision to hold its midterm convention in the state, the onslaught of GOP spending in the race is another clear sign the party is taking Talarico’s challenge seriously.

According to AdImpact, Republicans have now spent more on ads in the Texas Senate race than on any other non-presidential race on record. A total of $442 million has been spent on the race, including a record $326 million from Republicans and $116 million from Democrats.

Only the 2024 Ohio Senate race was more expensive, according to AdImpact, with a total of $543 million spent. But that race was more evenly divided between parties, with Republicans spending $296 million and Democrats spending $247 million.

Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., and its affiliates have spent at least $25 million boosting Paxton, according to campaign finance reports available this weekend. Those numbers do not take into account future reservations. Texas PAC, affiliated with the Senate GOP leadership, has contributed another $130 million to the race.

National Democrats are starting to invest in Texas , but on a much smaller scale. DDHQ’s chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley told Morning Report he’ll be watching whether the funding gap starts to show up in polls.

“As you see over the last month of this race this huge amount of money being spent in that race — and disproportionately it looks like it’s going to be Republican money — does that bring his numbers down, raise Paxton’s numbers a bit?” he said.

▪ The Hill : Trump heads to Texas as GOP worries mount over Paxton

▪ The Hill : Thom Tillis : ‘Almost statistically impossible’ for GOP to win House.

Trump announced a new partnership Tuesday to try to speed up the manufacturing of nuclear-powered submarines. The announcement came with the backdrop of wars around the world, which have heavily involved cheaper drones. I asked former Army Secretary Eric Fanning , who’s currently president and CEO of the Aerospace Industries Association, if we should be focusing more of our spending on drones.

“It’s not either-or. We get this question a lot. We debate this a lot. It’s both,” Fanning told me. “We do need more drones. There is a lot of investment taking place in drones, a lot of private sector companies investing in drones. It’s a great place for competition because of the cost point,” he added.

I asked that question because nearly every guest who’s discussed our military arsenal on the show over the past year has noted the cheap cost of drones and how we need to build those up to catch up with other nations. Still, our extensive nuclear triad is partly what sets us apart from the other militaries worldwide.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

Christa Pike is conscious and speaking days after she was given two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital during a botched execution in Tennessee. She had been incapacitated and on a ventilator in the aftermath of the execution as medical practitioners worked to save her life. The state has suspended executions for the rest of the year while it investigates what went wrong.

Paramount Skydance officially closed its multibillion-dollar deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday after a settlement was reached in a lawsuit from a dozen state attorneys general who challenged its legality. The merger will create the largest provider of news, sports and entertainment offerings in the world, to be known as Skydance.

Trump said repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are close to complete , and it should be refilled “this week.” He reiterated unfounded claims of vandalism causing setbacks in the pool’s repairs, allegations that have been rejected in court and contradicted by administration officials.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite/Robert F. Bukaty)

CLASH OF THE CANDIDATES : Candidates in several key midterm races sparred Tuesday evening in at-times heated debates as Election Day creeps closer.

In perhaps the most high-profile faceoff, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), one of Democrats’ top targets in the Senate this year, butted heads with former state Senate President Troy Jackson .

Collins sought to distance herself from the president as she seeks reelection in the blue-leaning state. She emphasized her position supporting abortion rights and her vote against Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year. Jackson pressed her on her crucial vote to advance the bill out of committee and her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh , who ultimately cast a deciding vote to overturn Roe v. Wade.

Collins said she looks to determine whether judicial nominees are “fit to serve” and sought to turn the tables on Jackson for his past more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career.

In Michigan, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) faced Rep. John James (R-Mich.) on stage for a gubernatorial debate.

Like Collins, James appeared eager to note clear differences with the president during the debate, which was hosted by Nexstar’s WOOD-TV. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

James said Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, but the war should have ended “yesterday.” Benson blasted him for voting six times against a war powers resolution calling on Trump to end hostilities.

James also called on U.S. and Canadian officials to return to the negotiating table amid the trade war and “stop acting like children.” He and Benson both expressed support for suspending the federal gas tax over high fuel costs at the pump.

Tensions were also on display at the Iowa gubernatorial debate between Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn , with accusations of carpetbagging and attacks over family wealth and culture war issues flying.

The candidates will participate in three more debates before Election Day, as Democrats try to win the Iowa governor’s mansion for the first time in two decades.

▪ The Hill : Sparks fly in first Iowa governor’s debate.

▪ The Hill : Planned Parenthood Votes adds $1 million to Maine, Michigan ads.

INFORMATION PLEASE : Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia to provide more information Tuesday about the suspected pneumonic plague outbreak following the death of a lab worker in Siberia.

Rubio told reporters during a trip to Iceland that Russia should show transparency with the rest of the world so countries can react “appropriately and accordingly.” The State Department reiterated its warning for Americans to not travel to Russia over the suspected outbreak.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said Monday that there are no further signs of infection at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, where the outbreak allegedly occurred.

WHO told NewsNation that all of the deceased worker’s contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness and that none have shown symptoms.

The agency said the current risk to the general population appears to be low, but the assessment will be updated once more information is available.

▪ The Hill : Five things to know as plague sparks COVID-19 memories.

▪ The Associated Press : How Russia, the world are responding.

RIVALRY RESUMES : California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) returned to his role as a chief antagonist to the president Tuesday following Trump’s remark that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if the regime develops a nuclear weapon.

Trump made the comments while defending the Iran war at a rally he held in Nebraska on Monday.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe,” Trump said of high gas prices during the war, adding that Iran could “take out a city.”

“Let ‘em take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego,” he said. “This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

Newsom slammed Trump as “deranged and dangerous” for the remark. He told The Hill’s Amie Parnes and Julia Manchester that the 25th Amendment should be invoked against the president.

The White House has disputed the interpretation of Trump’s comments, with communications director Steven Cheung saying the “media freakout” isn’t “rooted in reality.”

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President,” Cheung said on the social platform X.

▪ Reuters : Californians blast Trump remark.

▪ The Guardian : Republican congressional candidate rebukes Trump.

NO-CONFIDENCE : Cornell University’s faculty senate has cued up a vote of no confidence against the university’s administration amid backlash to its handling of an alleged gang rape of a student in 2024.

The faculty members will review the resolution next Wednesday, Oct. 14. It was led by Paul Ortiz , a professor of labor history at Cornell.

“As you may suspect, we were approached in our capacity as faculty senators by numerous Cornell colleagues demanding action. Many of these faculty–including myself–were approached by students at Cornell who are upset, fearful for their personal safety, and wanting our university to address the perennial problem of sexual assault on the campus,” the statement reads.

Cornell’s administration has faced intense scrutiny from politicians and the public for its oversight of the alleged gang rape that a female student reported took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house two years ago. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James (D) as a special prosecutor to look into the case.

Cornell also tapped former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of how the institution responds to sexual harassment and assault on campus.

▪ ABC News : Police received tip about fraternity trying to keep rape under wraps.

The president will make an announcement at 1 p.m. He will travel to San Antonio to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. EDT and then return to the White House.

Gen. Francis Donovan, commander of U.S. Southern Command, speaks during a forum of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition in Panama City, Aug. 12, 2026. (Matias Delacroix, Associated Press)

STEPPING UP : The Pentagon is expanding its multifront war against drug cartels in South America, embedding U.S. special forces on the ground in raids against traffickers among other moves, The Hill’s Filip Timotija reports .

“You dismantle the networks, attack network logistics, prevent adversary regeneration, bolster sovereignty and security and build a coalition,” a senior U.S. official told him. “So that’s the basis of a five-year plan.”

The Trump administration has been increasing pressure on the cartels since the president returned to office at the start of last year. The military has been blowing up alleged drug boats — and often those on board — in the Caribbean and East Pacific and interdicting refueling vessels off the coast of Ecuador before destroying them.

The administration has sought to improve its cooperation with countries in the Americas, creating a 19-member Americas Counter Cartel Coalition to oppose transnational organized crime.

That’s led to a partnership with Ecuador in which U.S. special forces have taken part in raids by Ecuadoran police on alleged drug traffickers.

The senior official said the U.S. will help train partner forces to aid in “command and control” operations on the ground.

Experts told Timotija that operations could soon be happening inside Colombia.

The U.S. Southern Command head, Marine four-star Gen. Francis Donovan , met with Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora in August in Tumaco, a port city located in the southwest corner of Colombia. That’s an area experts said is more likely to be targeted than near Colombia’s border with Venezuela.

▪ The Hill : Pete Hegseth to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln in San Diego.

▪ The Hill : US tries new Sudan strategy amid war fueled by ‘external actors.’

Israeli flags decorate rooms of Israelis who evacuated from cities and towns along the border with Lebanon, in kibbutz Ginosar hotel, northern Israel, March 5, 2024. (Ariel Schalit, Associated Press file)

SOLEMN ANNIVERSARY : Today marks three years since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel that claimed 1,200 lives and plunged the region into turmoil that continues to this day, even after a ceasefire went into effect last year.

Israel has already begun its ceremonies commemorating the day, as Oct. 5 of this year marked the anniversary on the Hebrew calendar. Two state ceremonies were held Monday at Mount Herzl, Israel’s national cemetery, while dozens of other memorial events were held throughout the country, The Jerusalem Post reported .

The October Council, a nonprofit founded by many of the family members of Oct. 7 victims and hostages, planned a moment of silence for 6:29 a.m. local time, when the initial attack began. Events are also taking place put on by the families of those killed at the Nova music festival.

The peace deal went into effect almost exactly a year ago following negotiations between Israel and Hamas, with the U.S., Turkey, Qatar and Egypt acting as mediators. Both sides have violated terms of the ceasefire since then, raising questions about the future of the deal in which Hamas is to disarm and eventually cede power.

The Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry has reported more than 74,000 Palestinians have died during the war, as of late last month. Strikes have occasionally continued even after the ceasefire went into effect, causing the death toll to tick up.

The anniversary also comes as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to face Israeli voters later this month for the first time since the attack and the war began. Netanyahu has faced intense backlash from critics for the security failures that allowed Hamas to carry out the deadliest attack in Israel’s history.

One recent poll found most Israelis view the Oct. 7 attack as central to their choice in the upcoming legislative elections.

Polls have shown a close race between the bloc led by Netanyahu and the opposition, with the possibility remaining that both sides could fail to win a majority of the 120-seat Knesset.

▪ The Times of Israel : Gadi Eisenkot challenges Netanyahu to televised debate.

▪ NPR : Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned ahead of Oct. 7.

Iran is losing — that’s why we should expect and prepare for more terrorist attacks , former national security adviser John Bolton writes in The Hill.

There’s another cockpit Israelis need to rush , Bret Stephens writes in The New York Times.

Emmy statues are seen at the 70th Primetime Emmy Nominations Announcements at the Television Academy’s Saban Media Center July 12, 2018, in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello, Invision, Associated Press file)

And finally … Another awards show is set to leave television for a streaming service, and this time with a dose of irony. The Television Academy announced Tuesday that the Emmys will be leaving broadcast networks for Amazon Prime .

The academy and Amazon announced it has reached a six-year deal to make the streaming platform the exclusive home for the Emmys, which are awarded annually for achievement in TV. The switch will start with next year’s ceremony, airing live.

A release states that the ceremony will remain free for viewers worldwide, forgoing Amazon’s paywall.

The Emmys are the second of the major awards that make up an EGOT to switch to streaming. The Academy Awards, also known as the Oscars, are scheduled to stream on YouTube starting in 2029 after ABC airs the 2027 and 2028 shows.

articles.title: US military aid to Israel continues three years into Gaza genocide
articles.summary: US military aid and arms transfer continue unchanged, as US public sentiment shifts.
articles.body:
Washington, DC – Three years into Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, little has changed in terms of official US support.

The government in Washington, under former President Joe Biden and current President Donald Trump, has continued near-complete unconditional military aid to Israel since October 7, 2023, even as the region has exploded into wider conflict, including the US-Israeli war with Iran.

The US aid has persisted even through periods when the administrations offered tame criticism of the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s military offensive in Gaza, repeated violations of a “ceasefire” reached last year, and roadblocks to a more lasting peace in the Palestinian enclave and wider region.

To date, at least 74,243 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, which killed at least 1,139 people. At least 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the October 11, 2025 ceasefire went into effect as Israel has continued to expand its area of control.

“The bottom line is that under both the Biden administration and the Trump administration, the US has continued to provide unconditional support for Israel, both in terms of finances, arms transfers and other forms, such as diplomatic support,” according to former Department of State official Josh Paul, who now runs A New Policy lobbying firm.

“That’s before we start adding in the costs of America’s wars in the region, whose causes are greatly attributable to our support for Israel and to Israel’s actions,” he said.

The United States has for decades offered Israel outsized military support and preferential access to US weapons, with Washington providing nearly $300bn in aid since its creation in 1948 when adjusted for inflation, more than any other country.

Washington has repeatedly codified support for Israel, most notably through a 2008 law that requires the US government to assure Israel maintains a so-called Qualitative Military Edge (QME) over its neighbours.

Because of that, Israel’s military remains deeply intertwined with the US government and US-made weapons, upon which it relies for its air force, several of its most devastating munitions, tanks and other military vehicles, as well as its Iron Dome, David’s Sling and Iron Beam air defence systems .

Rights groups, including Amnesty International, have repeatedly linked US-made weapons to civilian killings in Gaza and the wider region, although Israel has blocked independent monitors from entering the Palestinian enclave.

“Because Gaza is a genocide, and the US has supplied so much weaponry, there’s really no getting out of the fact that the US has a responsibility,” William Hartung, a defence analyst who has analysed US-Israel aid, told Al Jazeera.

Since October 7, 2023, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations to Israel, money that comes directly from government coffers funded by US taxpayers.

The most direct form of US military support comes from government appropriations to Israel, which account for $3.8bn a year under a 10-year memorandum of understanding signed by the administration of former President Barack Obama in 2016.

That $3.8bn was appropriated in fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026. The total figure also includes a towering supplemental security package of $14.1bn, passed by Congress and signed into law in April 2024.

The funding is predominantly made up of so-called Foreign Military Financing, which provides funds for US-made arms transfers and other services, and to a lesser degree, so-called offshore procurements, which provide funds for Israel to build its domestic arms industry.

Other portions of the funding are specifically allocated to replenish existing weapons stocks and maintain Israel’s air defence systems.

Israel also has access to a so-called War Reserves Stockpile, a programme that keeps a store of certain US weapons in the country, allowing for swift access upon approval from Washington.

Direct US government appropriations overlap with arms sales to Israel. Such sales – which must be approved by the US State Department, which in turn must notify the US Congress – can be paid for with US military aid or from other funding sources.

Nevertheless, Hartung says the vast majority of sales are paid for with US aid.

Sales can take years to deliver, depending on the availability and sophistication of the equipment being bought, entrenching the US and Israeli military in relationships long after the initial agreement.

“It’s a timeline where something approved today will do damage down the road, and the stuff doing damage now was approved some years ago,” he said.

To date, the US has approved at least $33.16bn in arms transfers to Israel since October 7, 2023, according to an Al Jazeera analysis of State Department notices to Congress.

Since the Israel military offensive began, the US State Department under both Biden and Trump has also repeatedly declared an emergency related to US national security interests when it comes to support for Israel, a rarely used legal manoeuvre that allows the administration to bypass some congressional oversight.

State Department-approved sales since October 7, 2023 have included thousands of rounds of 120mm tank munitions greenlit in December 2023 and again in August 2024, F-15 fighter jets and parts valued at $18.82bn approved in August 2024, and a $7.4bn package of bombs, guidance kits and fuses, and Hellfire missiles approved shortly after Trump took office in 2025.

At the time, Trump lifted a Biden-era pause on a pre-approved shipment of 2,000-pound (900kg) bombs to Israel.

Rights groups say the wide radius of the bombs, which can be up to a quarter mile (0.4km), causes widespread civilian devastation. A 2024 study found Israel dropped nearly 600 of 2,000-pound bombs across densely populated Gaza from October 7 to October 23, 2023.

In September, US Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he had placed a hold on a $2.8bn transfer of 40,000 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, saying he had not received assurances that the “weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians”.

Beyond weapons, three years into Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the US has also continued to offer diplomatic cover for Israel.

Before the October 11, 2025 ceasefire, that support showed up most clearly in the UN Security Council, where the US, as one of five permanent members, repeatedly vetoed resolutions calling for an end to the war.

All told, the US vetoed six separate resolutions related to Gaza, most recently in September 2025.

The US approach has since evolved into a pressure campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.

Trump initially announced plans to sanction the court and those who work with it in a February 2025 executive order. He charged the ICC had engaged in “illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel”.

The US has sanctioned a series of ICC officials, a UN rapporteur , and several Palestinian rights groups , with Secretary of State Marco Rubio promising in July to accelerate an “all of government” approach to dismantle the tribunal.

Joyce Ajlouny, general secretary of the American Friends Service Committee, has called the Trump administration’s approach “an affront to all victims and survivors of war crimes and genocide”.

Washington has taken other efforts to shield Israel from accountability.

The law appropriating the most recent round of military funding further blocks any US funding from supporting an independent commission launched by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 investigating the occupied Palestinian territory.

It also blocks US funding for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

While there has been little divergence from the executive branch in its unconditional support for Israel, the domestic political context in the US has shifted dramatically over the last three years.

A May New York Times/Siena poll found that about 68 percent of Democrats opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel, climbing from 45 percent three years earlier. A Gallup poll from February found that while 70 percent of Republicans sympathise with Israelis over Palestinians, the share had dropped by 10 percentage points compared with just a year earlier.

Lawmakers in Congress have increasingly reflected that discontent, even if resolutions seeking to block weapons transfers continue to fall short of the two-thirds majority in the House and Senate needed to take effect.

“Years ago, even an amendment to block a sale to Israel would have been unthinkable,” analyst Hartung said. “I think the tide is turning. But I mean, the killing’s happening now, so it’s not a lot of solace unless we really can stop it.”

US Senator Bernie Sanders and lawmakers in the House have introduced legislation to block weapons sales.

A fact sheet compiled by Sanders office in 2024 pointed to the reported use of US munitions, notably 120mm tank rounds, in several high-profile killings of civilians in Gaza, including five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza City, as well as the use of Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAMS) in several high-casualty Israeli strikes.

A bill to block the sale of military bulldozers received 40 votes in the US Senate in April 2024, in what some advocates hailed as a historic shift.

In September, 47 Senators voted to advance a bill that would require the State Department to conduct an investigation into US citizens killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank, which could eventually lead to restrictions on military aid.

On the opposite side, pro-Israel US lawmakers have sought to formally integrate the US and Israeli military in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for fiscal year 2027.

A version of the bill passed by the Republican-controlled House would boost technological cooperation between the US and Israel, potentially funnelling billions of dollars of US funds into Israel’s defence industry and circumventing congressional oversight.

In essence, the provision is an attempt to “transition the defence relationship from the annual appropriations cycle into the deeper machinery of the Defense Department contracting world”, according to A New Policy’s Paul, and in turn, sidestep changing public sentiment.

“[A relationship] that is less transparent, less susceptible to political pressure, and more deeply embedded in the US military-industrial complex,” he said.

articles.title: Congress is trading on your dime
articles.summary: Congress is the trustee of a government that just crossed $40 trillion in debt in August. It should live under the same rules we do, with no carve-outs and no riders.
articles.body:
In the film “Wall Street,” Gordon Gekko called information the most valuable commodity he knew of . Congress took that as a benefits package.

On September 30, the Senate voted 53-47 on a bill to limit lawmakers’ stock trading, seven votes short of the 60 needed to start debate. So the trading desk stays open.

I have spent more than three decades around other people’s money. Since 2015, I have been a designated expert witness in federal and state courts on what fiduciaries owe the people they serve. At a family office, a trustee who traded ahead of the investment committee would leave with a cardboard box and probably a subpoena.

Congress is the trustee of a government that just crossed $40 trillion in debt in August. Its members should live under the same rules we do, with no carve-outs and no riders.

The House passed the Stop Insider Trading Act, H.R. 7008, 232-198 on July 22, with 13 Democrats on board. It bars members, spouses, and dependent children from buying individual stocks . It requires public notice seven to 14 days before a sale. Chairman Bryan Steil (R-Wisc.) said it “ ensures no lawmaker can profit off of insider information. ” Critics note that it still lets members keep what they already own .

The bill also carries a photo ID requirement for voting . Senate Democrats called the ID language a poison pill and the trading limits too weak , so every Democrat in the upper chamber voted no. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called the bill “as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine.” Fair enough, but the vote only asked whether the Senate would begin debate. Senators who think the bill is weak could have opened it and deliberated it on the floor. Photo ID would pass tomorrow on its own vote. Bundling the two handed Democrats a ready excuse.

Judge Benjamin Cardozo wrote in 1928 that fiduciaries are held to “the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive,” and that conduct allowed between strangers is forbidden to them . The investment advisory industry applies a modest version. SEC rules require firms’ staff to report quarterly holdings and get approval before buying into initial public offerings.

Congress gets lighter requirements. Members sit through classified briefings and committee markups, and the STOCK Act of 2012 gives them up to 45 days to report trades. Business Insider found 49 members reporting their trades belatedly in 2020 and 2021 — why not, when the penalty starts at $200 ? Most were paperwork cases, as PolitiFact cautions . A rule that cheap invites nobody to read the fine print.

How well the information pays is an old and much debated question. A peer-reviewed study from 1993 to 1998 found that stocks senators bought beat the market by 85 basis points a month. In a May Economist/YouGov poll , 76 percent said members shouldn’t buy and sell individual stocks, with 77 percent of Republicans in agreement, and 41 percent said most members of Congress are corrupt.

The names are familiar. Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) has claimed through her office that she owns no stocks and has no knowledge of her husband’s trades. His 2026 House filings, one in June and one in August , list Intel call options valued at $1 million to $5 million, then July purchases of Intel and Bloom Energy stock and calls.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a Democrat who criticizes colleagues who trade , reported 5,402 trades in 2025 and carries an estimated net worth of $167 million. He says family trusts make the trades, not him.

Nobody here is charged with doing anything wrong — that’s the design flaw. Disclosure tells voters what happened, long after the fact.

The stakes track the scale. The Congressional Budget Office reported a $2.0 trillion deficit through August, with interest costs up $111 billion, or 12 percent . Its baseline put net interest at $1.0 trillion this year , above defense spending in every year it projects. Appropriations, tariff schedules, and defense contracts all move share prices, and members vote on every one of them. I backed DOGE and thought it stopped short. Audit the conflicts too.

The House bill is a start. Its penalty, the greater of $2,000 or 10 percent of the trade plus the gain, would sting, even if the grandfather clause would not. I would have them require divestiture or a blind trust within 180 days, cover spouses and dependents, cut the 45-day reporting window to two business days, and strip every rider. Keep the exemption for diversified funds , so members can still own the whole market. They just can’t pick winners from the rooms where winners get chosen.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has argued that a ban would drive off qualified candidates , and the pay complaint has some basis. Rank-and-file members last got a raise in 2009 , to $174,000, and inflation has trimmed that pay by about 33 percent in the time since. Still, they campaigned for the job and knew the salary going in.

If $174,000 is too little, argue for a raise in the open. Sunlight beats a side hustle.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: Red states exude confidence after Supreme Court climate arguments
articles.summary: Two Republican-led states say their massive lawsuits against social media and drug companies are no permission slip for the blockbuster fossil fuel industry lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court this week. “When you look at our opioid cases, they went directly at the problem,” Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall (R) told The Gavel. “If you…
articles.body:
Two Republican-led states say their massive lawsuits against social media and drug companies are no permission slip for the blockbuster fossil fuel industry lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court this week.

“When you look at our opioid cases, they went directly at the problem,” Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall (R) told The Gavel.

“If you look, I just settled the case with TikTok for $300 million two weeks ago, directly with a company that we believe was creating harm for children,” he continued.

On Monday, the Supreme Court opened its term with arguments on whether cities and states can leverage their courts to force the energy industry to pay billions in damages for allegedly contributing to climate change.

The lawsuit from Boulder, Colo., notably doesn’t target greenhouse gas emitters. That would’ve had a more uphill climb under a 2011 Supreme Court precedent .

Instead, the city is suing producers: ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy.

The companies say it’s preempted by federal law and the Constitution. In his final comments to the justices, the companies’ lawyer insisted that the city’s legal theory could ultimately leave an everyday American exposed to liability when they cross the border into Colorado and fill up their gas car.

We caught up with Kevin Russell , Boulder’s attorney who argued the case, as he was leaving the Supreme Court Building on Monday. He rejected the other side’s notion.

“There are serious questions about under state law how who can be held liable and under what circumstances,” Russell said. “A ruling in our favor in this case isn’t going to mean that every person who’s gassing their cars up is going to be liable.”

“They want to regulate what someone does in my state. They want to regulate any state, anywhere in the world. They want to regulate if it takes place in Saudi Arabia — those actions are impacted here,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown (R), who traveled to the nation’s capital for the argument in support of the companies, told us.

“And so that’s the real issue, is that to what extent do we have one state trying to dictate policy for many other states.”

He and Marshall sounded optimistic upon exiting the building. They noted Justice Brett Kavanaugh ’s suggestion that the court’s precedents potentially provide a straightforward win for the companies and moments at which Chief Justice John Roberts posed tough questions to Boulder.

“If you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” the chief justice predicted. “They’ll probably copy your pleadings.”

Still, the court tussled with several overlapping issues during the 107-minute argument Monday. Justice Clarence Thomas repeatedly asked if the court had jurisdiction to hear the companies’ appeal or needed to throw it out.

It left both sides exuding confidence as the court begins work on its opinion.

That may not land until next year, but the Republican attorneys general still see it tying into affordability issues this campaign cycle.

“They’re the same people who are complaining about the price of gas, or just energy generally,” Brown said of the plaintiffs. “[They] have done something that is going to dramatically — if they’re successful — dramatically increase the price of energy for everyone in America.”

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams. Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Alito becomes an author: Samuel Alito has joined the ranks of Supreme Court justices who are published authors. His book came out Tuesday, and Zach got an advance copy. Read his analysis here .

Another shake-up for Seattle prosecutor: An appeals court panel paused a directive for the Trump administration to reinstate Roger Rogoff as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle.

Reflecting Pool case permanently dead: The Justice Department will not be allowed to recharge Olympic canoeist David Hearn over now-dismissed accusations he vandalized the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a judge ruled.

No Trump name carving at USIP: A federal appeals court ruled that President Trump’s name can’t be permanently carved into the U.S. Institute of Peace building, for now.

Smith’s game-day texts, revealed : Text messages obtained by our colleague Rebecca Beitsch show the communications Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) used to erroneously accuse special counsel Jack Smith of attending an NBA game in Atlanta — an effort to tie him to a Georgia prosecution of Trump — didn’t reference any basketball team names.

Alito says don’t expect lame-duck retirement: In an interview with Bloomberg Law , Alito said he expects to serve out this Supreme Court term, casting aside any speculation that he will try to retire before the change of power in January, if Democrats retake the Senate in the midterms.

Judge’s suspension fight moved : Suspended U.S. Circuit Judge Pauline Newman just got a win. The judge remains suspended for refusing her colleagues’ demand to submit to mental fitness testing three years ago. The Supreme Court previously turned away her appeal to resume hearing cases , but newly unsealed court documents show that Chief Justice John Roberts has ordered future misconduct proceedings be handled by judges in the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, rather than the Federal Circuit, where Newman serves. She had long sought the transfer.

The Trump administration’s clashes with the media at the White House and beyond is back in the federal courts in Washington, D.C., this week.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan had pointed questions for the Justice Department on Tuesday morning, as lawyers tried to defend the Federal Communication Commission’s (FCC) decision to initiate an early review of eight ABC stations’ broadcast licenses.

The Trump administration argues that the process, called for by FCC Chair Brendan Carr in April, was necessary as part of the department’s probe into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion hiring practices. Disney owns ABC.

But a lawyer representing the media giant cast that inquiry as merely “pretextual” and accused the government of engaging in a “retaliatory campaign” to punish the network for unfavorable coverage.

AliKhan, a Biden appointee, appeared skeptical of the administration’s justification but did not rule from the bench. Read the story from Sophie and Media, Sports and Politics Reporter Dominick Mastrangelo for a deeper dive .

Later that afternoon, a three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit heard oral arguments in a challenge brought by the National Association of the Deaf (NAD) over the White House’s decision to stop providing sign language interpreters at press briefings and public events.

The organization and one of its members sued the Trump administration in May 2025, arguing that the move unlawfully discriminates against individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing (DHH).

U.S. District Judge Amir Ali ordered the White House in November to immediately restore real-time American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation for all briefings conducted by President Trump or the press secretary.

“The district court thus found, as a matter of fact and on a well-established record, that plaintiffs and many other deaf persons across the country were being discriminated against on the basis of disability as a result of the defendant’s conduct,” a lawyer representing the NAD said.

The administration has since launched a dedicated YouTube channel to comply with that order but also appealed.

Pews in the E. Barrett Prettyman Courthouse annex courtroom were filled for arguments, and the presence of many DHH individuals prompted the court to temporarily alter its strict electronics policy so attendees could follow online closed captioning.

An ASL interpreter was also stationed at the front of the room, and a large screen transcribed the proceedings in real time. These battles are ongoing as several media organizations are also fighting for unimpeded access to the White House grounds.

Lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS NOW will be back in U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ’s courtroom Thursday to ask for a preliminary injunction that would bar the administration from enforcing a ban against the outlets.

Last month, Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that directed the Trump administration to restore network reporters’ press credentials, finding that the ban likely violated their constitutional due process rights. That order lasts only two weeks.

The administration has advanced a familiar argument to justify the president’s decision, citing national security concerns. But the outlets have pointed to Trump’s comments indicating that the ban was based on negative coverage as evidence of viewpoint discrimination, which is prohibited under the First Amendment.

The ban has impacted pool coverage of the president’s daily activities, as the White House has since barred CNN and Politico from fulfilling its duties several times by restricting access to Air Force One.

Cases the Supreme Court is taking up — or passing on — this term.

The Supreme Court took up three cases this past week, a relatively low number for the first conference back of the new term.

The headliner is Trump’s mandatory detention policy.

In Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha , the justices will wade into the avalanche of litigation nationwide concerning whether the administration can legally detain people found to be in the country unlawfully as their deportation proceedings unfold — without giving them a bond hearing — even if those people had been living in the U.S. for many years.

The second case is one we’ve also previewed in The Gavel. If you ever wanted to see the high court take a divorce case, you have your wish.

In Marschner v. Marschner, the justices will review whether a couple’s divorce settlement is preempted by the Uniformed Services Former Spouses’ Protection Act. The settlement had made financial guarantees to the ex-wife if her ex-husband later waived his military retirement pay to receive disability benefits.

And the final case involves religious zoning.

In Missionaries of Saint John the Baptist v. Frederic , the court will decide if an Ohio city’s zoning regulations that prevent a group from building a religious grotto violate federal religious liberty protections.

The Supreme Court turned away roughly 800 cases Monday. We’ll choose just one to highlight.

The justices declined to take up D.A. v. Tri County Area Schools, a First Amendment appeal from two brothers punished by their Michigan school district for wearing sweatshirts to class that read “Let’s Go Brandon,” a phrase used to mock former President Biden .

Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito — two of the court’s leading conservatives, who last year publicly said the court should’ve heard another student’s case who tried to wear a shirt that read, “there are only two genders” — said nothing this time.

The Supreme Court wants the Trump administration to weigh in before it decides whether to take up several of the other cases we’ve highlighted in past editions.

That’s the prognosis for the three mortgage escrow interest cases — Citizens Bank v. Conti , Cantero v. Bank of America and Flagstar Bank v. Kivett — as well as the antitrust cases we previewed — AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP v. Mosaic Health Inc. and United Biologics LLC v. Amerigroup Tennessee Inc.

The justices also want the administration’s thoughts on the case about whether a Native American tribe can sue a mining company under the federal Superfund law for damages over cultural loss it experienced from the company allegedly contaminating the river. The case is Teck Metals v. Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation .

Petitions for the Supreme Court to take up cases we are keeping a close eye on…

Now, onto more petitions being considered this coming week that the justices could take up.

MIT antisemitism accusations: Two Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) students and a group aimed at fighting antisemitism seek to revive their civil rights lawsuit against MIT, which claims Jewish students have been subject to antisemitic harassment amid anti-Israel protests. Lower courts ruled they had no legal claim. The case is StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. MIT .

Cay Clubs executive: President Trump commuted the 40-year prison sentence given to Dave Clark, a former Cay Clubs executive convicted on bank fraud and obstruction charges. It left intact, however, a requirement for him to pay hundreds of millions in penalties. Lower courts rejected Clark’s effort to wipe them and denied him a certificate of appealability, which he needs to try to appeal certain arguments. He says he should’ve been given one. The case is Clark v. United States . The justices are asked to take up a similar legal question in a lower-profile case, Berry v. United States.

Medical course implicit bias requirement: An ophthalmologist who teaches continuing medical education courses in California — which physicians must complete every two years to keep their license — is challenging a requirement that courses address implicit bias. She says she’s a private actor being compelled to speak in violation of the First Amendment. The lower courts dismissed her suit, ruling it is government speech. The case is Khatibi v. Yip.

Police power exception: The justices are mulling three cases concerning whether a police exception exists to the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause, which requires the government to provide just compensation when it takes private property. The underlying cases involve car impoundments in Chicago and police raids elsewhere. The cases are O’Donnell v. City of Chicago , Hadley v. City of South Bend and Pena v. City of Los Angeles .

Illegal immigration & double jeopardy: It’s a felony to reenter the U.S. illegally after being deported. Jesus Herrera-Salazar, a Mexican national, did so and was convicted. Then, law enforcement found him unlawfully in the country — again. He argues that unless the government can prove he crisscrossed the border a subsequent time, they can’t show it’s a different crime, so it violates double jeopardy protections. The case is Herrera-Salazar v. United States .

Michigan police shooting: Two Lansing, Mich., police officers seek to end an excessive-force lawsuit after they fatally shot a man, who was reaching for a gun, while responding to a domestic disturbance call. The case raises issues of qualified immunity and constitutional use-of-force protections. The case is Moore v. Romero.

The Supreme Court will hold oral arguments in Department of the Air Force v. Guahan , a dispute over the Air Force’s practice of denotating WWII-era munitions on Tarague Beach in Guam.

A federal judge in the Southern District of New York will hold a hearing in the criminal case against Gannon Ken Van Dyke , a U.S. soldier accused of betting on military operations in Venezuela.

Another federal judge in New York will consider The Intercept’s bid to block Truth Social’ s API, which gives customers quicker access to the president’s posts for a cost of up to $100,000 per month.

A closed settlement conference will be held in the U.S. Court of International Trade for an update on the $166 billion in refunds of IEEPA tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court. The government disclosed Tuesday that it has so far sent $126 billion to the Treasury Department for disbursement.

A federal judge in D.C. will hold a preliminary injunction hearing in CNN, Politico and MS NOW’ s bid to retain press access to the White House.

Cilia Flores , the wife of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro , will appear in federal court in New York as she seeks to be released from jail ahead while awaiting trial on drug trafficking charges.

A hearing will be held in Nashville after Dolly Parton ’s estate was granted a temporary restraining order against her nephew and his security company.

Federal courts are closed for Columbus Day.

The Supreme Court will release an orders list and hold oral arguments in Beaird v. United States , a case examining how much deference should be given to commentary in federal Sentencing Guidelines

Jury selection will begin in the federal death penalty trial for Payton Gendron , the gunman charged with killing 10 people and wounding three others in a racially motivated attack at a Buffalo, N.Y., supermarket in 2022.

articles.title: Is America experiencing Trump Saturation Syndrome?
articles.summary: America’s media, even when not deliberately negative, as they are with Trump, are overwhelming.
articles.body:
As President Trump’s approval ratings languish, could the root of his problem be overexposure?

Both the anti-Trump and the pro-Trump camps seize on ways to explain his falling poll numbers. Opponents wish to attribute his fall to his policies ; supporters want to blame media bias for his ills. Instead, might the answer be oversaturation — that he has been over-exposed to the Americans who fall between these two camps?

National polling shows Trump’s job approval ratings are falling. According to RealClearPolitics’ national polling average, as of yesterday, Trump’s approval rating was just 38.5 percent, versus 37.7 percent for George W. Bush and 43.3 percent for Barack Obama at the same point in their second terms.

To his critics’ charge, Trump’s approval does lag on the issues . Yet less than two years ago, he won a resounding triumph on those same issues. Voters chose him, and they chose him by his biggest vote in his three presidential runs. It was a resounding rejection of the Biden-Harris policies of the previous four years.

To his supporters’ claims: Yes, the establishment media report on Trump negatively. According to a Media Research Center analysis of the first 100 days of Trump’s second term, the media’s coverage was 92 percent negative. Simultaneously, the media downplay anything positive that Trump accomplishes.

Yes, there is the ongoing conflict with Iran and yes, inflation is continuing its over five-year run above the Fed’s preferred level. Yes, Trump’s arrest of Nicolas Maduro and his deals with Venezuela and Greenland are wins for America. But is there something running between both political poles?

Although Trump is in his second term, a nonconsecutive second term is a rarity in American politics. He has not had six consecutive years in office, as Bush or Obama had. What Trump does have, which neither Obama nor Bush did, is three consecutive runs for president — winning twice and narrowly losing once. No American politician has accomplished this feat on a major party ticket since Franklin D. Roosevelt, 84 years earlier.

This means Trump has been at the forefront of America’s national political stage since 2016. And his trifecta has brought with it an unimaginable level of scrutiny.

America’s president has been a national headline since at least Roosevelt — day in, and day out. Yet the press was different then. So, too, was the media cycle. It was not as pervasive and all consuming, nor was it coming in through a plethora of devices. Roosevelt had radio, print and movie newsreels. He also had a news cycle that ended, in contrast to today’s unceasing one.

The media was far more limited then and imminently more controllable. Yes, Roosevelt had his friends and foes and let each one know it. America was on the cusp of World War II in Roosevelt’s third run and at war throughout his third term and when he ran in 1944. America’s press was far more subservient to the commander in chief in general, particularly so in time of acute crisis.

Our press is none of those things now. Yet even aside from this, there is an issue of inundation. America’s media, even when not deliberately negative, as they are with Trump, are overwhelming. Through their variety of entry points, they saturate us.

If there is any doubt, imagine a public figure who has been one for any duration — not Warhol’s 15 minutes, but a thorough and prolonged immersion in the media landscape. Admit it: Unless you are an absolute fan, you’re sick of him. You would happily never hear another word about him or see another picture. You’ve had your fill. But still, the media keeps presenting him.

This happens to everyone in the media’s lens to some extent, but Trump takes this to another level. The Trump Saturation Syndrome hypothesis is that those who are not diehard supporters or opponents — those in between — have begun to check out.

Trump is hardly blameless for his condition. No one has craved media attention so much or proved so adept at garnering it. This was true before he entered political life. Once he attained what Teddy Roosevelt called the “ bully pulpit ,” it only metastasized.

Trump tweets incessantly, comments on everything, attends every major event and holds regular press conferences. There is not a day when he is not front page news on every outlet; it is often multiple headlines and multiple times a day.

In this wake of unprecedented coverage for a historically high duration, has the bulk of the nonaligned electorate simply said enough? Has America reached the saturation level with Trump, and perhaps, with any president?

After all, we have now had three consecutive one-term administrations. This after a period when one-term administrations were rarities in American politics — there were only two of them elected between 1936 and 2016 .

Maybe no politician can withstand the level of intense, uninterrupted — and yes, hyperpartisan — scrutiny that the American presidency and our divisively partisan political climate now entails.

J.T. Young is the author of the recent book, “Unprecedented Assault: How Big Government Unleashed America’s Socialist Left” from RealClear Publishing.

articles.title: Trump is on the cusp of toppling Brazil’s leftist giant
articles.summary: Trump has brought down the giant of the Latin American Left, and “21st-century socialism” is in intensive care.
articles.body:
In May, President Trump welcomed Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro to the White House. That meeting changed everything. Last Sunday, Bolsonaro won in the first round with 47 percent of the vote, ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who received 45 percent.

What happened in Brazil is no coincidence. Following Trump’s return, at least seven Latin American countries have taken an unprecedented turn to the right. Twenty years of socialism in Bolivia came to an end. Dictator Nicolás Maduro was captured. Chinese influence over the Panama Canal waned. The Shield of the Americas Security Alliance was formed.

Yet the jewel in the crown arrived this Sunday with Bolsonaro’s first-round victory in Brazil’s elections. President Trump put it this way : “Well, it’s a big victory: close, but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”

What happened in Brazil wasn’t just an election; it was a landslide defeat. Although he has not yet lost his office, Lula has already lost control of Brazil’s Congress, Senate , districts and mayoralties large and small . Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Lula’s predecessor as president, now heads into the Oct. 25 runoff as a heavy favorite.

The stories of Trump and Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, share many similarities. Both lost bids for re-election. Their supporters were accused in both cases of an alleged coup, and both faced serious legal battles. However, while Trump achieved both judicial and political victory, the elder Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison .

President Lula believed that imprisoning Jair Bolsonaro would put an end to the right-wing movement. He was wrong; it only made the movement stronger. As the 80-year-old president’s political standing eroded — amid a failure to resolve issues of crime and violence — the desire for change grew unstoppably.

Last Sunday, four members of the Bolsonaro family secured extraordinary victories. His wife, Michelle and son Carlos won Senate seats, and his son Jair Renan and brother Renato won seats in Congress. The political trials and persecution directed at the Bolsonaro family catapulted their popularity, translating it into votes.

The polls had gotten it wrong. Lula was intoxicated with power and convinced he would win in the first round — or, at worst, finish first and head toward a highly favorable runoff. Those responsible for gauging the public mood never accounted for the people’s deep-seated weariness and their silent cry for radical change.

Lula, who has run for the presidency at least seven times since 1989 , had exhausted all his tricks. His populist playbook — cutting the workday, betting on expanded welfare programs like Bolsa Família, raising wages and promising to protect the Amazon and gay rights — failed to deliver. Lula failed to read the writing on the wall. By the time he did, it was too late.

The socialist leader’s greatest mistake was underestimating the Brazilian people. They had witnessed firsthand the Venezuelan migration crisis, and the damage that socialist populism could inflict — even on a nation possessing the planet’s largest oil reserves .

As in many Latin American countries, security was the main concern . Soft-on-crime policies, especially toward organized crime, had failed spectacularly. Lula’s strategy of engaging in dialogue with or attempting to reintegrate hardened criminals into society was viewed as a betrayal of the public; it seemed to protect aggressors while mocking victims.

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s security model continues to gain followers across Latin America. Bolsonaro said that Bukele inspires him because he has achieved “one of the greatest and most effective restorations of sovereignty and public security.”

Another factor contributing to Lula’s defeat is his outdated rhetoric against the U.S. He staked everything on class struggle , anti-imperialism, rejecting the dollar and pinning hopes on the Chinese yuan. He also advocated for state control over social media , credit cards and online betting — a dangerous communist-style model for censoring and controlling the population.

Lula was the last dinosaur of Cuban-style socialism. His Workers’ Party was founded a year after the Sandinista Revolution, and Lula was always an admirer of Nicaraguan dictator Daniel Ortega, who just abolished elections in his country. The idea for the São Paulo Forum originated in Managua during Lula’s first meeting with Fidel Castro.

Lula’s defeat is no coincidence. A wave of change is sweeping across the Americas, where security and alliances with the U.S. have taken on new significance and are translating into electoral victories.

Trump is about to bring down the giant of the Latin American Left, and “21st-century socialism” is in intensive care. This is excellent news.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.

articles.body:
The Supreme Court will hear arguments Wednesday about which environmental requirements the government must follow when handling unexploded World War II-era munitions in Guam.

For decades, the government has brought the munitions to Andersen Air Force Base. It agrees it must follow the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, which lays out procedures specifically for hazardous waste.

But the U.S. Air Force faces a lawsuit insisting it must also adhere to the mandates of the National Environmental Policy Act, a more generic statute that requires federal agencies to assess environmental impacts before major projects.

The Air Force brought the case to the Supreme Court after an appeals court revived it.
