articles.title: ‘Moral majority’ no more: The Republican Party’s criminal desperation
articles.summary: So much effort has been dedicated to protecting politicians like Max Miller and Donald Trump that it appears Republicans ran out of time to do anything else.
articles.body:
If you want to see the face of real Republican desperation, look no further than President Trump’s local Republican Party.

Republican leaders in Palm Beach, Fla. are so fearful of a November blue-wave election that they are considering extreme steps to protect their hold on power — including refusing to cut ties with an elected official arrested for alleged child sex abuse .

Palm Beach County Clerk of Courts Mike Caruso told the Miami Herald he still “intends to win” his race, despite being arrested in August and subsequently suspended from office. State officials swiftly withdrew their support from Caruso’s re-election campaign, but the Palm Beach Republicans still have Caruso’s back.

It is enough to make any decent Floridian gag.

It was fitting that the Miami Herald broke its story on Oct. 5, the same day that disgraced former House Speaker Dennis Hastert (R-Ill.) died . Hastert spent 15 months in federal prison for violating banking laws in an effort to cover up his admitted history of sexually abusing boys as young as 14.

The only difference is that Republicans had the self-respect to cut ties with Hastert when his own scandal broke. The same cannot be said for a party still shamelessly clinging to Caruso.

After decades spent selling out their values in order to preserve their power, Republicans have shed so much of their basic decency that they finally have no guiding principles left. The rise of Trumpism and its anything-goes view of ethics proved to be the final nail in the coffin of a party that was already well on its way to moral hollowness. One can only hope a drubbing in November will give Republican leaders cause to reflect on the ineffective and self-serving abomination their party has become.

Speaking to a room full of conservative donors earlier this year, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson made clear that the only thing keeping corrupt Republicans out of jail was the fact that he personally “ run[s] the protection program ” in Washington. “I’ll take care of you,” Johnson promised his financiers. So much for subtlety.

Under the new values-free party, any candidate meets their non-existent standard for office, so long as they say they are a Republican. Holding power is all that matters, even if Republicans themselves have admitted for nearly a year now that they are unwilling and unable to use that power in ways that improve the lives of regular Americans.

The domestic abuse scandal that recently consumed Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) offered Republicans one last opportunity to rediscover their consciences, but the lure of power prevailed once again. Court documents revealed a mountain of serious allegations against Miller, from throwing hot water on his ex-wife Emily Moreno’s chest to holding a gun to her head and even fracturing his daughter’s collarbone.

In one court document, Miller’s 2-year-old daughter turned to her mother and remarked, “Daddy kill you.”

Miller responded with trademark Trumpian sleaze. In addition to denying the allegations, he publicly suggested he would release damaging personal information about his former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). He also defiantly refused to end his re-election bid, reasoning (correctly, it turned out) that his fellow Republicans would ignore even the most extreme allegations of abuse if it meant holding on to a critical House seat.

Last month, House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) reiterated that Miller “is our nominee right now,” though she hopes “the allegations weren’t true.” The House Speaker has also remained staunchly in line behind Miller after the White House urged Republican lawmakers to swallow their morals and shut up about Miller’s problems.

“We’re gonna support our nominees,” Republican National Committee chairman Joe Gruters said in an interview with NewsNation back in August. “We need to make sure we hold the majorities.”

For what? What good is a legislative majority to a party that believes in nothing and politicians who tout family values messaging while standing behind candidates accused of child molestation and jaw-dropping levels of domestic abuse?

For a party that is as morally and legally compromised as today’s Republicans, a governing majority is only useful as a tool to protect their own members from meaningful accountability. It offers nothing to the rest of us but a textbook example of how the corrupt turn government into a tool of their own impunity.

The 119th Congress has worked less and passed fewer bills than any Congress in more than 50 years. So much effort has been dedicated to protecting politicians like Miller and Trump that it appears Republicans ran out of time to do anything else. In one final, flagrant “screw you” to the very idea of public accountability, Johnson even recessed his do-nothing House until after Election Day — all to avoid bringing to the floor articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Trump, Johnson and the MAGA Republicans in Congress have screamed for months that a Democratic wave election would bring with it a wave of Republican arrests. If Democrats do win back power in November, they’ll find no shortage of deserving perps.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies .

It was fitting that the Miami Herald broke its story on Oct. 5, the same day that disgraced former House Speaker Dennis Hastert (R-Ill.) died . Hastert spent 15 months in federal prison for violating banking laws in an effort to cover up his admitted history of sexually abusing boys as young as 14.

The only difference is that Republicans had the self-respect to cut ties with Hastert when his own scandal broke. The same cannot be said for a party still shamelessly clinging to Caruso.

After decades spent selling out their values in order to preserve their power, Republicans have shed so much of their basic decency that they finally have no guiding principles left. The rise of Trumpism and its anything-goes view of ethics proved to be the final nail in the coffin of a party that was already well on its way to moral hollowness. One can only hope a drubbing in November will give Republican leaders cause to reflect on the ineffective and self-serving abomination their party has become.

Speaking to a room full of conservative donors earlier this year, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson made clear that the only thing keeping corrupt Republicans out of jail was the fact that he personally " run[s] the protection program " in Washington. "I'll take care of you," Johnson promised his financiers. So much for subtlety.

Under the new values-free party, any candidate meets their non-existent standard for office, so long as they say they are a Republican. Holding power is all that matters, even if Republicans themselves have admitted for nearly a year now that they are unwilling and unable to use that power in ways that improve the lives of regular Americans.

The domestic abuse scandal that recently consumed Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) offered Republicans one last opportunity to rediscover their consciences, but the lure of power prevailed once again. Court documents revealed a mountain of serious allegations against Miller, from throwing hot water on his ex-wife Emily Moreno's chest to holding a gun to her head and even fracturing his daughter's collarbone.

In one court document, Miller's 2-year-old daughter turned to her mother and remarked, "Daddy kill you."

Miller responded with trademark Trumpian sleaze. In addition to denying the allegations, he publicly suggested he would release damaging personal information about his former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). He also defiantly refused to end his re-election bid, reasoning (correctly, it turned out) that his fellow Republicans would ignore even the most extreme allegations of abuse if it meant holding on to a critical House seat.

Last month, House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) reiterated that Miller "is our nominee right now," though she hopes "the allegations weren't true." The House Speaker has also remained staunchly in line behind Miller after the White House urged Republican lawmakers to swallow their morals and shut up about Miller's problems.

"We're gonna support our nominees," Republican National Committee chairman Joe Gruters said in an interview with NewsNation back in August. "We need to make sure we hold the majorities."

For what? What good is a legislative majority to a party that believes in nothing and politicians who tout family values messaging while standing behind candidates accused of child molestation and jaw-dropping levels of domestic abuse?

For a party that is as morally and legally compromised as today's Republicans, a governing majority is only useful as a tool to protect their own members from meaningful accountability. It offers nothing to the rest of us but a textbook example of how the corrupt turn government into a tool of their own impunity.

The 119th Congress has worked less and passed fewer bills than any Congress in more than 50 years. So much effort has been dedicated to protecting politicians like Miller and Trump that it appears Republicans ran out of time to do anything else. In one final, flagrant "screw you" to the very idea of public accountability, Johnson even recessed his do-nothing House until after Election Day — all to avoid bringing to the floor articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Trump, Johnson and the MAGA Republicans in Congress have screamed for months that a Democratic wave election would bring with it a wave of Republican arrests. If Democrats do win back power in November, they'll find no shortage of deserving perps.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies .

articles.title: Rubio sounds campaign-ready as he rails against open borders, globalism in speech from ancient Greek ruins
articles.summary: Marco Rubio will deliver a major address near the Acropolis calling on Americans and Europeans to reject decline and renew Western civilization.
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio took aim at open borders and globalism Wednesday in a sweeping speech in Athens, Greece that at times sounded more like a campaign stump speech than a foreign policy address. "We opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay," Rubio said against the backdrop of the sun setting on the ancient citadel in Athens. "The word nationalism became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments, we condemned our own history, and in too many places we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit," he continued. "And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control." Rubio and Vice President JD Vance have both been widely discussed as potential successors to Trump in 2028, with the president himself repeatedly fueling speculation over which of the two could inherit his political mantle. Rubio argued the consequences were now playing out in an increasingly dangerous world. TRUMP’S COUNTERTERRORISM STRATEGY SCORES BIG WINS AGAINST GLOBAL TERROR THREATS "As the West's confidence faltered, its adversaries and rivals only grew more assertive," he said. Rubio called the current moment an "inflection point," warning that the threats facing the West are "every bit as real as they were during antiquity." "And now there is war again. There is competition between great powers again," he said. Rubio singled out Iran as he drew a sharp distinction between Western values and those of its adversaries. "Fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself," Rubio said. "Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but our heroes do not worship death," he went on. "It is precisely because we value life, that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles." The secretary of State delivered the address from the Acropolis, using the birthplace of Western civilization to trace America's own inheritance from Ancient Greece. "For twenty-five centuries since, the Parthenon has stood. Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow," Rubio said. "Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now, I stand here today – as the Secretary of State of that republic, and as the great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space, can ever extinguish." Rubio said he saw signs that Europe was beginning to reverse the trends he described. "We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago," Rubio said. "There are already signs. Across this continent, we are witnessing the beginning of what we hope will be a generational shift." During his visit, Rubio announced a new counterterrorism partnership between the U.S. and Greece. He emphasized the strategic importance of Greece on Wednesday, calling it a "source of stability in an unstable world." "As you see a world that faces these destabilizing events, you recognize how important this alliance with Greece is to the United States," Rubio said. "It is a source of stability in an unstable world." At the Munich Security Conference in Germany in February, Rubio delivered a speech on the topic that earned him a standing ovation from European leaders, and racked up millions of views online. One popular X user described it as "one of the greatest" speeches by a Secretary of State in decades. Many others insisted the speech upped Rubio's potential 2028 presidential chances. AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US Rubio described the five centuries before the end of World War II, a time when the West had expanded across the globe, building "vast empires." But, he said, after the war, Europe was in ruins, and "godless communist revolutions" in Europe caused people to believe that the West's dominance was forever finished. "Against that backdrop, then, as now, many came to believe that the West's age of dominance had come to an end, and that our future was destined to be a faint and feeble echo of our past. But together, our predecessors recognized that decline was a choice, and it was a choice they refused to make," he said. Rubio urged the European leaders to reinvigorate that spirit. "This is why we do not want out allies to be shackled by guilt and shame," he continued. "We want allies that are proud of our culture and our heritage, and understand that we are heirs to the same great and noble civilization and who together with us, are willing and able to defend it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And this is why we don't want allies to rationalize the broken status quo, rather than what is necessary to reckon with what is necessary to fix it. For we in America have no interest in being polite and orderly caretakers of the West's managed decline. We do not seek to separate, but to revitalize an old friendship and renew the greatest civilization in human history."

articles.title: Why Paramount-Warner merger has sparked fears about press freedom
articles.summary: Chairman’s family ties to Trump and Israel raise questions over editorial independence at CNN and CBS.
articles.body:
Paramount Skydance has completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, bringing CNN and CBS News under the same corporate ownership, in a deal that has raised concerns about editorial independence and freedom of speech.

The acquisition, worth about $110bn including debt, combines two of Hollywood’s biggest studios after months of legal challenges lodged by state attorneys general and unions.

The new company, Skydance Corporation, brings together HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network, alongside streaming services Paramount plus and HBO Max.

But its control of two major US news organisations has drawn particular scrutiny. David Ellison, Skydance’s chairman and chief executive, has promised to preserve their editorial independence, but his father, Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison is a major financial backer of the deal, and has previously donated funds to US President Donald Trump and Israel.

Asked about the takeover on Tuesday, Trump welcomed it. “They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company,” he said.

The takeover faced initial opposition from Hollywood workers, politicians and state prosecutors concerned about the mounting concentration of power in an industry already dominated by a handful of companies.

Netflix initially reached an agreement to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery. Paramount then launched a competing bid, prompting a bidding war before Netflix walked away.

A California-led coalition of 12 state attorneys general sued to block the deal, saying that it would reduce competition and raise prices. The Writers Guild of America brought a separate challenge.

Both cases were settled in September when Paramount agreed to commitments relating to film production, support for displaced workers and protections for the news networks, including the creation of a new editorial independence board.

But the settlement did not end opposition to the deal. “This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost people their jobs,” actor and activist Mark Ruffalo has said.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren linked the takeover to Trump’s efforts to restrict media access. “As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” she said, referring to the US president’s so-far thwarted attempt last month to bar reporters from several news organisations , including CNN, from accessing the White House.

Can an editorial independence board protect CNN and CBS?

One condition of the settlement requires Skydance to establish a “News Editorial Independence Board” within 180 days of completing the takeover.

The five-member body is to include active or retired journalists with at least 10 years of experience. It is intended to establish editorial principles and address disputes involving the news networks and corporate management.

However, its members will be appointed by, and will report to, Skydance’s board of directors, which Ellison chairs. Two members can belong to the same political party, and there is no requirement to publish its findings.

The condition has left critics with a multitude of questions, including: How can a member of an independent editorial board be a member of a political party? How can there be scrutiny if its findings are not public? How can it be independent if it is appointed by a board of directors, themselves appointed by the CEO of the company?

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said, “A Paramount-appointed editorial independence board for CNN and CBS is worthless. The fish rots from the head, and this particular fish is headed by a compromised oligarch with a history of throwing journalists under the bus to advance his business interests.”

Stern also questioned whether government enforcement of the settlement could itself threaten press freedom. “The editorial board creates the same First Amendment problems it’s supposed to solve – the government meddling in the news.”

The First Amendment provides constitutional protection for freedom of speech and the press.

Ellison argues that the two networks will continue to operate independently. “We’re going to make sure that CNN and CBS News are completely editorially independent,” he said on Tuesday.

On Monday, Skydance announced that Mark Thompson would remain CNN’s chairman and editor-in-chief, while Bari Weiss will continue as CBS News’s editor-in-chief, easing previous fears that Weiss would immediately take charge of both networks.

Why are there fears for editorial independence?

The takeover gives the Ellison family control of CNN less than a month before the November 3 US midterm elections, and follows Trump’s repeated attacks on the network as it seeks to hold the US president to account.

Shortly after Paramount launched its bid in December, Trump accused CNN of spreading “poison and lies” and said it was “imperative” that it be sold, while the Trump administration has moved to bar CNN from reporting in certain areas of the White House.

Ellison donated roughly $45m to a political nonprofit group supporting Trump’s election efforts in 2024, while he donated $16.6m to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, a charity supporting Israeli soldiers – its largest single donation at the time.

Earlier this year, the White House criticised CNN’s coverage of the US-Israeli war on Iran, while Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”

Sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates also hold indirect financial interests in the combined company. They have no voting stakes, although their involvement adds another layer of scrutiny over its funding.

Concerns about the future for editorial integrity, however, intensified after Skydance acquired Paramount in 2025, and layoffs followed, alongside the closure of CBS News Radio and changes to CBS News flagship investigative programme 60 Minutes.

High-profile firings enacted under CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss and Skydance Media CEO David Ellison included correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, as well as 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon.

The programme’s September season premiere attracted about 21 percent fewer viewers than a year earlier.

In 2025, Paramount also agreed to pay Trump $16m to settle a lawsuit over the editing of a 60 Minutes interview with then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

In a June 2 letter, nine advocacy groups, including Reporters Without Borders, the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Committee for the First Amendment, warned that CNN could face similar upheaval and firings.

“Bari Weiss’ shameless actions fulfil the Ellisons’ commitment to President Trump to remake CBS to his liking,” they alleged, referring to the firings and changes at 60 Minutes.

“Larry Ellison has reportedly promised to do the same at CNN if allowed to take control through the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Not because it makes any business sense, but because they seek to control the public discourse.”

The groups described the proposed takeover as an “existential threat to the free press, independent media, and free speech in this country and beyond”.

articles.title: When will 2027’s Social Security COLA be announced?
articles.summary: It won’t be long until we know how much benefits will increase by next year.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – October is an important month for Social Security beneficiaries, especially those already looking ahead to next year.

Not only will some receive two payments this month — all because November starts on a Sunday — but all recipients will learn just how much their benefits will change in 2027.

Every year, the Social Security Administration announces a cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, which is designed to help recipients of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) retain their buying power amid rising inflation. The COLA is usually released in conjunction with the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index (CPI).

More specifically, it rolls out alongside the CPI data for September, which is released in mid-October.

The COLA was thrown off that schedule last year amid a government shutdown .

At present, there is no government shutdown, so the COLA for 2027 is expected to be announced on Wednesday, Oct. 14.

Until then, we won’t know exactly how large the COLA will be.

Estimates from The Senior Citizens League have fluctuated slightly throughout the year. In April, TSCL projected a 3.9 percent increase . By August, that had fallen to 3.6 percent . Last month, the projection was at 3.5 percent .

A COLA anywhere in that range would be an increase over the 2.8 percent Social Security recipients saw for 2026 .

Any adjustment will first impact your January 2027 benefits. For some, however, that payment may come in December.

The Social Security Administration follows a regular payment schedule for all of its beneficiaries. Payments may come earlier than expected if the intended disbursement date falls on a weekend or holiday.

Jan. 1, New Year’s Day, is considered a holiday, meaning the first 2027 payment for those who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will be paid on Dec. 31, 2026. The same is true for those who received Social Security before May 1997, or receive both Social Security and SSI.

Nexstar’s Michael Bartiromo contributed to this report.

articles.title: Tillis defends insulting Trump officials: ‘I stand by all that’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Tuesday defended insults from his new political memoir thrown at Trump administration officials, saying he stands “by all that.” CNN’s Kaitlan Collins read off Tillis’s “unsparing” remarks from “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” starting with the North Carolina Republican saying his vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Tuesday defended insults from his new political memoir thrown at Trump administration officials, saying he stands “by all that.”

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins read off Tillis’s “unsparing” remarks from “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” starting with the North Carolina Republican saying his vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “the biggest regret” of his career.

“You admit that you should have stopped [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.] from becoming health secretary,” Collins continued. “You say [former Director of National Intelligence] Tulsi Gabbard won’t be challenging anyone for president of her local Mensa chapter. You say [ex-Homeland Security Secretary] Kristi Noem’s a dog murderer and that [Commerce Secretary] Howard Lutnick ‘is nuttier than squirrel s‑‑‑.'”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“I stand by all that,” Tillis responded. “What else you got?”

The senator, who is retiring at the end of the term, said he supports “the majority of people” in the president’s Cabinet. Collins pushed back, saying his comments hit the majority of top Trump administration officials.

“The point is we hired them, we made a decision to put them in there,” he replied. “I’m giving them their annual review. They didn’t pass, you cycle them out.”

Tillis added, “Get somebody else, get somebody that can tell the president the truth, set the priorities right and get us reelected. That’s all this is about.”

Criticisms aside, he argued Trump is a populist who will do “a good job of bringing out that base that’s uniquely motivated by him” to vote in the upcoming November midterm elections.

“Traditional conservatives, traditional Republicans have to do their part to get the other folks out and say, ‘Guys, we’re dealing with populism just like the Democrats did with Biden and with Obama. And we’ve got to get through it. But you don’t abandon your party,'” the Republican added.

Tillis wrote in his book that he does not have “beef” with the president, only with “the idiots he’s got working for him,” The Associated Press reported before the book’s release on Tuesday.

The GOP lawmaker has stood apart from some of the White House’s positions and proposals in the past, including Trump’s immigration agenda. He recently said he agreed with his Senate Republican colleagues that mass deportations have gone too far , noting that the president’s support among Hispanic voters has dropped since 2024.

“I would rather have 100 illegally present people go free than have that innocent person caught,” he previously told The Hill.

Tillis said Monday that, with the book’s release, he was “not at all” concerned about possible retaliation from the White House, particularly after Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) phone number to Truth Social after he opposed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent.

The senator told ABC’s “The View” that the book includes private text exchanges between him and the president, noting that with “all due respect, I got his number too.”

articles.title: The Catholic Church is benefiting from the Leo effect
articles.summary: Catholic dioceses across the U.S. have reported record numbers of conversions.
articles.body:
In September, Pope Leo XIV didn’t just travel to France. He conquered it. Approximately 300,000 people lined the streets of Paris as the Popemobile traveled to the newly restored Cathedral of Notre Dame de Paris. Another 600,000 people attended an open-air mass presided over by Pope Leo. And 80,000 attended a youth vigil where all available spots were filled within hours of opening.

Most importantly, during this past Easter there were more than 21,000 adult baptisms , a record for the French Catholic Church.

Something similar is happening in the U.S. Catholic dioceses across the U.S. have reported record numbers of conversions. In Los Angeles, there was a 139 percent increase , Phoenix saw a 23 percent increase and New York saw a 36 percent increase. In Leo’s home archdiocese of Chicago, there was a 52 percent increase — the highest number of conversions since 2013.

Even smaller dioceses , such as those of Rapid City, S.D., and Fairbanks, Alaska, saw a sizeable number of converts.

Many converts were young people between the ages of 18 and 35 . A spokesperson for the Diocese of Boise, Idaho noted that they were drawn to the “transcendent beauty, clarity, and orthodoxy of the Catholic faith.” Archbishop Mitchell Thomas Rozanski of St. Louis says , “In our age of uncertainty, and in our age of great anxiety, [there] is a thirst and hunger for God and stability that faith brings to people’s lives.”

A survey of Catholic converts from 20 dioceses confirms those findings. Eighty-four percent said they were interested in exploring a deeper spirituality or relationship with God, 77 percent wanted to grow in goodness and virtue, 72 percent wanted a greater sense of inner peace and 56 percent wanted to belong to a church community that united believers around the world and across generations.

The record number of Catholic converts coincides with the 2025 election of Pope Leo XIV. During his first year as Pontiff, nearly eight in 10 U.S. Catholics approve of Pope Leo, with 32 percent expressing extremely favorable views.

In 1995, Harvard Sociologist Robert Putnam wrote a path-breaking article titled “ Bowling Alone: America’s Declining Social Capital .” What Alexis de Tocqueville once called a nation of joiners , Putnam discovered had become a nation of loners. Illustrative of this change was the declining number of those joining bowling leagues and, instead, bowling alone. In the mid-1960s, American bowling peaked with 12,000 alleys open across the nation. By 2023, that number diminished to a mere 3,154 . Americans weren’t just bowling alone; they weren’t bowling at all.

In France, 22-year-old Jonas Tauitou-Faron says that his age group is “trying to search for meaning in the current world, and some of us are finding religion.” Leo agrees, noting that in a secular society young people “ are obviously searching for something .”

Joining the Catholic Church involves more than fulfilling a Sunday obligation to attend mass. Church involvement builds community and social ties. One of the new Catholic converts, 19-year-old Jesse Araujo of Pahrump, Nevada, said what drew him to the faith was listening to Catholic podcast stars he found on YouTube.

Amen-Ra Pryor, a 23-year-old student at Howard University, started college during the pandemic and struggled with depression and finding community. For him , the Catholic Church’s teachings on suffering were especially helpful when he was going through difficult trials.

Robert Putnam notes the positive effects of joining a church. In his book, “Our Kids: The American Dream in Crisis,” he writes that those involved in their church communities “have better relations with their parents and other adults, have more friendships with high-performing peers, are more involved in sports and other extracurricular activities.”

At some of the “ hot Catholic churches ” such as St. Joseph’s in New York’s West Village and St. Patrick’s Old Cathedral in Nolita, young people mingle at post-Mass wine receptions.

Traveling the U.S. in 1831, Tocqueville noted that in a nation that placed a premium on equality, there were “ some very dangerous propensities .” Among them were isolating citizens from one another, concentrating attention on oneself and opening the soul to “an inordinate love of material gratification.” Religion, he concluded, was a perfect antidote that inspired “diametrically contrary principles.”

By promoting communitarian values, Tocqueville believed religion helped foster democratic principles. And even if a particular faith did not save men in another world, “ it is at least very conducive to their happiness and their greatness in this. ”

Addressing the Catholic converts in France, Pope Leo said , “I see not only the fruits of the Holy Spirit, you set you on this path, but also the promise of fruitfulness for the Church.”

“In turn, be missionaries of the Gospel in this society!”

It is this missionary spirit that is reinvigorating the Catholic Church. It is the antidote to what former U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy called “an epidemic of loneliness and isolation.”

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics.”

articles.title: Former CIA officer John Kiriakou's unexpected second act: From whistleblower to viral sensation
articles.summary: John Kiriakou discusses his transformation from whistleblower to viral sensation, gaining a younger audience through podcasts, social media and candid commentary.
articles.body: John Kiriakou spent 15 years working in the shadows as a CIA officer. Today, at 62, he's walking the runway at New York Fashion Week, racking up millions of views across social media and becoming an unlikely Gen Z internet sensation. His videos regularly attract millions of views, and his audience of hundreds of thousands of followers has transformed the former intelligence officer into an unexpected voice for a generation that was too young to remember the events that once defined his life. "I never thought that I would be this figurehead for thousands and thousands of young men between 15 and 35," Kiriakou told Fox News Digital. That newfound popularity has opened doors he never imagined, including one into the fashion world. Kiriakou is the first to admit he has never considered himself fashionable. During the interview, he joked that the black T-shirt he was wearing cost about $12 and said he only occasionally flipped through GQ to see what men were wearing. Yet in September, he found himself walking the runway for designer Elena Velez at New York Fashion Week — an unexpected appearance for a man better known for the CIA, national security and exposing the agency's interrogation program. HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL "I'm 62 years old. When in life am I ever going to get the chance to be on the catwalk at New York Fashion Week?" he said. Velez, whose runway shows are known for avant-garde fashion and unconventional casting, reached out after hearing Kiriakou's appearances on several podcasts. But the runway is only one chapter in what has become an unlikely second act. His online popularity accelerated after appearing on Steven Bartlett's "The Diary of a CEO" podcast. Clips from the interview spread rapidly across social media, introducing millions of younger viewers to stories from his years inside the CIA. For many members of Gen Z, Kiriakou represents a world they never experienced firsthand. He joined the CIA in 1990, serving as both an analyst and counterterrorism officer before leaving the agency in 2004. His online reach now extends well beyond short-form videos. Kiriakou also connects directly with supporters through Cameo, where users can purchase personalized video messages. Long before he became an internet personality, Kiriakou was at the center of one of the most contentious national security controversies of the post-9/11 era. In 2007, he publicly discussed the CIA's use of waterboarding during the war on terror. He later pleaded guilty to one count of intentionally disclosing information identifying a covert CIA officer and was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison. CIA WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS OBAMA-ERA ESPIONAGE CHARGES AGAINST HIM WERE A TEST RUN FOR TARGETING TRUMP Many of the young people who now follow him, however, know him first through viral videos rather than the headlines that once defined his career. Most were born after the September 11 attacks and did not experience those events as they unfolded. Kiriakou believes that generational distance is part of what draws Gen Z to his story. "There is a special place in my heart for Gen Z," he said. "It's because of Gen Z that I’ve been able to turn my life around and to do things that I had, for the last 62 years, never thought I could do." Kiriakou believes his growing popularity reflects something larger than internet algorithms. He said many young Americans are increasingly skeptical of traditional politics and are searching for voices they view as more authentic. "Gen Z has the largest number of political independents of any generation," Kiriakou said. "They don't like the Democrats. They don’t like the Republicans because they feel like they’re being lied to." Kiriakou, who described himself as an "equal opportunity hater," said he believes frustration with both parties has made younger audiences more willing to listen to voices outside the political establishment. "I think that's why I’m popular with Gen Z — because I’m seen as somebody who’s telling them the truth," he said. He argues that his appeal isn't rooted in perfection, but in transparency. Rather than trying to present himself as flawless, Kiriakou said he speaks openly about government, politics and his own personal mistakes. "I have literally nothing to lose," he said. "I have nothing to gain by lying." That willingness to speak candidly, he said, has allowed him to build an audience that stretches across the political spectrum. Despite his criticism of modern politics, Kiriakou remains optimistic about the next generation. "I think that these are real leaders in waiting," he said. "I think they're the ones who are going to save the country." His confidence in Gen Z is shaped in part by his own improbable second act. The life Kiriakou leads today bears little resemblance to the one he expected after leaving the CIA. In addition to hosting a podcast, he has advised a royal family in the Persian Gulf and is set to appear in an upcoming movie. "I never thought that I would walk in New York Fashion Week, that I'd be an advisor to a royal family in the Persian Gulf, that I’d have my own podcast," he said. "I never thought that I’d act in a Hollywood movie." FORMER CIA AGENT JOHN KIRIAKOU REVEALS HOW SEX PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE IN ESPIONAGE AND SPYING Those experiences have reinforced a lesson he now tries to pass along to younger people: don't be afraid to pursue opportunities that fall outside the life you originally envisioned. For young people uncertain about what comes next, he said the answer is often simpler than they think. "You just have to grab it," he said. "Grab it and do it. And have fun and enjoy yourself." Kiriakou's online following has also given him a new audience for issues he believes will shape the future, including artificial intelligence and national security. During his interview with Fox News Digital, he warned that AI is advancing faster than governments are prepared to manage. "This is the new frontier, AI," Kiriakou said. "It’s developing so quickly." TRUMP LAUNCHING 'SUPER INTELLIGENCE FORCE' TO ENSURE AMERICAN DOMINANCE From his perspective, the technology presents two major risks. One is the possibility that artificial intelligence eventually becomes difficult for humans to control. The other is the growing ability of foreign adversaries to weaponize AI against the United States. "There are two things to worry about here," he said. "One is that AI goes out of control, but two, it’s that our enemies use AI against us." Kiriakou said the United States has not kept pace with those emerging threats. "We’re not prepared. No, we’re not," he said. He pointed to one example that concerns him most: the impact AI could have on undercover intelligence operations. As facial recognition and biometric technology continue to improve, he questioned whether intelligence officers operating under aliases will be able to remain anonymous. "How in the world do undercover CIA officers or undercover intelligence officers from any country cross borders now or go through airports in an alias, in disguise?" FOLLOW US ON X Kiriakou argued that the United States should continue investing in both defensive and offensive AI capabilities while also building stronger safeguards around the technology before its development outpaces existing security measures. Questions surrounding national security have also remained central to Kiriakou's own legal battle. He is seeking a presidential pardon related to his conviction for disclosing classified information. His message to President Donald Trump: "Barack Obama, Eric Holder and John Brennan ruined my life, and Donald Trump is the only person who can give it back to me," Kiriakou said. Kiriakou said what happened to him is part of a broader debate over government secrecy, whistleblowers and public accountability, issues he said also influence his views on artificial intelligence and modern surveillance. articles.title: US, WHO request details from Russia amid reports of second pneumonia case
articles.summary: The WHO and the U.S. State Department have pressed Russia for more information about the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague institute.
articles.body: Amid global public health concerns surrounding the death of an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East worker, the World Health Organization noted in a statement issued Tuesday on the X account of Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus that it had requested more information from Russia regarding the matter, including on "media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause." "The individual died on 2 October 2026 after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia. Initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an alleged accidental laboratory exposure," the WHO statement noted. "In response to WHO’s verification request under the International Health Regulations, the Russian health authorities reported that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast. They informed WHO that an epidemiological investigation had been conducted, preventive and control measures implemented, and identified contacts placed under medical observation and tested. They reported that no high-threat pathogens had been detected among the contacts and that medical observation of all identified contacts had been completed," the statement explained. "WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," the statement notes. Reuters reported that when questioned about the WHO's request to respond to reports of a second individual in Siberia allegedly becoming sick, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called for caution when it comes to media reporting. "There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," Peskov said, according to the outlet. TRUMP SAYS PUTIN CALL COMING 'VERY SOON' AS US TRACKS SUSPECTED PLAGUE DEATH IN RUSSIA The U.S. State Department has formally requested more information from the Russian government regarding the death of the woman who worked at the anti-plague research facility, issuing what is known as a démarche, defined as a request or intercession with a foreign official. "We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government," a U.S. State Department spokesperson noted. "We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information." Fox News Channel senior foreign policy correspondent Gillian Turner reported that State Department health experts had been in touch with Russia's foreign ministry about the public health matter since Friday, but that the démarche arose due to Russian officials being unforthcoming via back channels. RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE 'FAR WORSE' THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) noted in a post on Tuesday that the "CDC is aware of and closely monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia that resulted in a death. We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available. "While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early. Pneumonic plague can spread person-to-person through respiratory droplets during close contact, which is why rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals, are important public health measures. TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP' "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely," the CDC's post concluded. Fox News Channel's Nick Kalman and Gillian Turner contributed to this report.

articles.body:
David Urban, a former adviser to President Trump, panned the president’s recent comments suggesting Iran could target Los Angeles and San Diego if the regime successfully builds a nuclear weapon.

“I do think that was a clumsy, sloppy kind of statement,” Urban told CNN’s Anderson Cooper in an interview Tuesday. “Obviously, he’s riffing there. I don’t — I think that … this administration’s intention the entire time has been to preclude Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, so that it could do anything against any U.S. city in the future.”

“And so, while it was crude and kind of rough and tumble and he kind of laughed about it, I don’t think the president meant it,” he continued.

Trump earlier this week defended the ongoing military operation in Iran , despite increased energy and cost-of-living expenses. He told GOP supporters during a rally in Nebraska that without the U.S. pressure, the Islamic Republic could seek to “take out” the two cities.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe,” the president said Monday evening, adding that Iran could “take out a city.”

“Let ‘em take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego,” he continued. “This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

The White House rebuffed critics’ framing of the comments.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote Tuesday on social platform X .

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” he continued. “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”

California Democrats , including lawmakers, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria and Gov. Gavin Newsom have blasted the rhetoric as “dangerous.”

The Golden State delegation in Congress also pressed the Trump administration for an apology as Newsom called for them to invoke the 25th Amendment.

articles.title: Paxton: Iran war a drag on Texas Senate campaign
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in the Lone Star State, said in a leaked audio recording that the war in Iran and high prices at home are a drag on his midterm campaign. “It’s not tariffs. … It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” Paxton told donors and lobbyists…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in the Lone Star State, said in a leaked audio recording that the war in Iran and high prices at home are a drag on his midterm campaign.

“It’s not tariffs. … It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” Paxton told donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser, according to audio shared by Axios , when asked what issues were “dragging” on his campaign.

“When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch. So I’d say that’s probably the biggest problem, and that pinch drives up food prices and everything else,” the Republican Senate hopeful said.

“That’s by far our biggest problem, and I think that’s why we’re having a hard time with numbers.”

It’s the latest sign of Paxton acknowledging a tough midterm election landscape, after The New York Times first leaked an audio clip of the same meeting in which Paxton said Republicans’ first-ever midterm convention in Dallas last month “dropped our numbers.”

A Paxton campaign spokesperson told Axios that “this is a non-story” and that Paxton acknowledged “what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high.” The Hill has reached out to Paxton’s campaign for additional comment.

Paxton, who won the GOP Senate nod in Texas over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R), is now trailing Democrat James Talarico by 2 percentage points ahead of the general election, according to Decision Desk HQ’s latest polling averages. Cook Political Report considers it a toss-up, despite Texas Democrats’ losing streak in statewide races.

President Trump is heading back to Texas Wednesday for his third visit to the state in a month, including the GOP’s Dallas convention. Paxton is expected to speak at a rally in San Antonio , which he said he hopes will “keep Texas red and Keep America first.”

But voter frustration with the economy, the war in Iran and immigration are dragging down Trump’s approval rating, raising questions about whether he’ll ultimately help or hurt Republicans in tough races this cycle.

articles.body:
President Trump wants to add a Camp David-type presidential retreat at his West Palm Beach, Fla., golf club, according to several reports.

A letter sent to Palm Beach County commissioners by the golf course’s attorney Harvey Oyer said Trump is offering to “designate” his golf course as a “U.S. Presidential Golf Course” and be “utilized by all past, current, and future United States Presidents and visiting foreign heads of state,” according to The Palm Beach Post.

The letter to the commissioners said Trump International Golf Club would pay for the construction of the presidential lodging facility.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents. It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors,” the letter said.

Oyer told The Washington Post that a name has not been selected for the presidential golf course yet.

“It would further cement Palm Beach County as one of the most recognizable brands and destinations in the world,” Oyer told the Post.

Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told the outlet that the county is seriously considering the proposal.

This isn’t the first time that Palm Beach is being considered for a spot for presidents. American businesswoman Marjorie Merriweather Post, who owned Mar-a-Lago and gave it its name, wanted the estate to be used as a place for presidents to go in the winter.

She gifted the property to the federal government upon her death in 1973, but the National Park Service found the upkeep to be too expensive and returned it to her estate.

Trump bought the property in 1985 and kept its name.

Trump’s golf course is less than 5 miles from Mar-a-Lago.

A White House official with knowledge of the plan told the Post that the golf course would provide “world class property” amenities.

“The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly-rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat,” the official said.

articles.title: AI-generated child sexual abuse images cause real-life harm
articles.summary: We should not wait for an AI-generated fantasy to become a real child’s nightmare to act.
articles.body:
Leaders of artificial intelligence firms have gotten attention recently for saying AI could someday end humanity . It’s unfortunate they’re not getting the same attention for a more immediate danger: AI is already making it easier to create and spread depictions of the sexual abuse of children.

That’s got to stop now. A federal appeals court recently agreed but ruled that the current state of the law prevents law enforcement from prosecuting people who use AI image generators to create what is often called “synthetic child pornography.”

But “pornography” is really the wrong word. “Pornography” describes sexual material created by consenting adults; children cannot consent to sexual abuse or its depiction. The more accurate term is child sexual abuse material, because that language makes clear what these images and videos actually depict: the sexual abuse and exploitation of children.

These materials can be lifelike depictions of toddlers engaged in sex acts with adults, or anything else you can imagine. But the court ruled that because the images don’t depict actual sexual abuse crimes against real children, they are free speech protected by the First Amendment.

The court urged state legislatures and Congress to catch up with the times, and it’s right. Until that happens, children all over the country are at risk. There are several reasons for this. The first is that these materials exist on a pathway that starts with obsession and often ends with real-life abuse. The pathway from obsession to abuse is not hyperbole. It is the way the mind works in other areas, too.

We understand in other contexts how repeated exposure can reinforce compulsive behavior, intensify fixation and drive people to seek increasingly extreme material. The same concern exists here: AI-generated child sexual abuse material can provide an endless supply of increasingly graphic content, feeding and escalating dangerous sexual fixations rather than interrupting them.

We should not wait for that fixation to result in the abuse of a real child before we take it seriously.

There is also harm built into how AI-generated synthetic child sexual abuse images are created. When generating synthetic content, AI learns from enormous collections of existing images and uses it to generate something new. That means photos of real children can become part of the tapestry these systems draw from to create realistic depictions of child sexual abuse.

AI-generated images and video can also involve a singular, specific and very real child, when it takes the form of a deepfake — when AI takes an image of a real child and manipulates it to make that child appear sexually explicit or to depict sexual abuse.

This remains illegal, but that has not stopped these tools from being used to victimize real children — as in the case of a group of Tennessee teenagers in which a man used Grok to digitally undress underage girls and then spread those images far and wide on Discord and Telegram, where they were sometimes bartered for other images of child sexual abuse.

It can get even worse than that, as one survivor found out, to her horror, when her own stepfather created new explicit materials based on past images of her child sexual abuse that existed online — aided by Grok, the AI tool from Elon Musk’s company xAI. People with a sexual obsession with children escalate when existing content doesn’t satisfy them.

Musk said last year he was “not aware of any naked underage images generated by Grok. Literally zero.” But his lack of credibility and his cruelly juvenile attitude toward such imagery— including suing Minnesota for its legislation banning “AI nudification” — makes him not worthy of belief. And the same is true of his peers in the AI industry.

I used AI chatbots myself, identifying that, as the founder of Lauren’s Kids , I am an advocate against child sexual abuse. I then asked how to become a perfect predator and groom children for abuse. These tools gave me chilling advice: to take my time and target children from single-parent families who might be economically disadvantaged, dealing with mental health challenges, substance abuse and so on. Any vulnerability would do. They also told me to be helpful, but not too helpful. They told me what to say if a child protests.

It was a bespoke guidebook for trainee abusers, created in seconds.

This cannot keep up. We must make changes. First, laws at the state and federal levels must catch up to reality, to make all creation of child sex abuse images with AI tools a crime. But even before then, the platforms must shut it down instead of pretending it doesn’t exist.

Creation of images like these should be banned by platforms. Attempts to create them should trigger alerts and immediate reports to law enforcement if protections are somehow skirted.

All of us — every parent and caregiver — must educate ourselves and our children to use AI responsibly, speak up if aware of a problem and involve trusted adults as soon as they can.

This simply is not a First Amendment issue. The law already recognizes that free speech protections have limits, including for certain forms of incitement and obscenity. AI-generated child sex abuse imagery should not be protected simply because technology can manufacture it without a camera.

We should not wait to act until after an AI-generated fantasy to becomes a real child’s nightmare.

Lauren Book is the founder and CEO of Lauren’s Kids, which prevents child sexual abuse through education, advocacy and awareness.

articles.title: Democrat launches ad featuring Moreno ripping GOP’s Miller over daughter’s blue bunny
articles.summary: Democrat Brian Poindexter’s campaign is launching an ad Wednesday featuring Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) criticizing his former son-in-law, Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), over an incident involving Moreno’s granddaughter’s stuffed blue bunny. The ad, first shared with The Hill, comes as Miller has faced intense scrutiny amid abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. She has…
articles.body:
Democrat Brian Poindexter’s campaign is launching an ad Wednesday featuring Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) criticizing his former son-in-law, Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), over an incident involving Moreno’s granddaughter’s stuffed blue bunny .

The ad, first shared with The Hill , comes as Miller has faced intense scrutiny amid abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. She has accused the House Republican of hurling hot water at her, pointing a gun at her head and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. Miller has denied the allegations and is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee.

The ad features remarks the senator made to reporters in August about his granddaughter crying at night because she did not have her stuffed blue bunny while staying with him. He claimed that Miller had refused to give the toy back.

“Look, I don’t care about the politics of this. My granddaughter, she has a little blue bunny that she sleeps with. Max would not hand over the little blue bunny. Literally held it hostage for 48 hours. This girl is crying at night because she can’t sleep without her little blue bunny. And his answer is, ‘I’m just not going to give it to you.’ So this is the level of total and complete depravity,” the senator said in remarks used in the ad. “Truly the seventh level of hell.”

Miller has previously denied that he kept the bunny from his daughter. The Hill has reached out to Miller for comment.

The ad also features images of headlines and excerpts from news reports about the dispute, including a Mother Jones headline that reads, “Rep. Max Miller has a history of withholding his daughter’s blue bunny,” and the opening of a Christian Science Monitor story that reads, “A missing blue bunny. Scalding hot water. A toddler watching it all.”

The ad is part of a broader Democratic effort to tie Miller to criticism from fellow Republicans as he faces a competitive reelection fight in a district President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has shifted the race from likely Republican to toss-up, while the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) has stepped up its support for Miller. The NRCC and Miller campaign combined for a three-week, more than $450,000 ad buy that began Sept. 7, according to Politico.

Ohio Democrats are planning to spend at least $500,000 on a series of mailers featuring Republican senators criticizing Miller, according to a source familiar with the plans.

Images of the mailers, first obtained by The Hill, show quotes from several Republican senators, including Sen. Tim Sheehy (Mont.), who called Miller a “degenerate sociopath,” and Sens. Jon Husted (Ohio) and Roger Marshall (Kan.), who have called on Miller to resign.

One of the mailers reads, “The facts are adding up against Max Miller, who has been credibly accused of violence against girls and women multiple times over the span of decades. Even other Republicans aren’t buying Miller’s denials over a wide range of charges.”

Poindexter told The Hill in a statement, “Voters deserve the facts, and the fact is that both of Ohio’s Republican senators have said Max Miller is unfit to serve. The people who know him best say he should not represent us in Congress.”

Abigail Angelos, a spokesperson for Miller, previously told The Hill, “The good people of the Ohio 7th district are standing behind Congressman Miller and the recent support from the NRCC confirms the party is standing behind him as well.”

“He looks forward to returning in November,” she added.

articles.title: GOP Michigan Senate candidate Rogers calls for trade war with Canada to end ‘now’
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) on Wednesday called for an end to the U.S.-Canada trade war fostered by the Trump administration, a sign of how the battle may be hurting his campaign against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) on Wednesday called for an end to the U.S.-Canada trade war fostered by the Trump administration, a sign of how the battle may be hurting his campaign against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

“Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war — now,” Rogers said in an ad he shared to social media .

Before that, the former representative noted that drinking a Labatt, a Canadian-made beer, and watching the NHL’s Detroit Red Wings “just doesn’t get any more Michigan.”

El-Sayed has blasted the trade war with Canada as “making things more expensive,” as inflation remains above 3 percent amid the Iran war .

Rogers had previously defended the tariffs as “necessary,” telling USA Today last month they were not a “one-size-fits-all solution.”

The Republican Senate nominee did not mention President Trump. Since August, Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have engaged in a tit-for-tat tariff war .

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The president first imposed 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods in August, with Carney matching those import taxes “dollar for dollar” in early September.

Trump has also threatened 50 percent tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting on Jan. 1.

Those levies, and a potential Canadian response, would hit Michigan particularly hard.

Businesses in the Wolverine State import $43.5 billion worth of goods from Canada annually, with cars, trucks and motor vehicle parts accounting for roughly 48 percent of that total, according to data from the Canadian government.

Trucks, cars and motor vehicle parts are also the top products Michigan exports to Canada, accounting for $10.2 billion of the $21.2 billion worth of products state businesses send to Canada.

Rogers is also not the only Republican to call for an end to the economic dispute between the U.S. and its second-largest trading partner.

Rep. John James (R-Mich.), who is running for governor, said Tuesday he has urged U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to return to negotiations with Canadian officials.

“We must get back to the table, stop acting like children and negotiate a reciprocal, fair and mutually beneficial arrangement,” James said during Nexstar’s WOOD-TV debate between him and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D).

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), whose state also borders Canada, has also publicly opposed the trade war.

In his new 30-second ad, Rogers also went after El-Sayed for backing tax hikes. The former Wayne County health official backs raising taxes on capital gains and wealth held by trusts, along with exempting individuals making up to $50,000 from federal taxes.

articles.title: 30 days and 5 takeaways on the midterms
articles.summary: As the midterm elections approach, analysts suggest that Democrats are well-positioned to flip the House due to shifting voter trends and enthusiasm despite significant Republican spending.
articles.body:
The month before the midterm elections is when most of the gray hairs emerge from the scalps at the two House congressional campaign committees. Nearly two years of strategizing, recruiting, messaging, mobilizing, analyzing and tabulating come down to a final sprint. It’s also the most perilous time: that last-minute “dark-money dump”; a smear attack; the gaffe by one of your own candidates that lands with all the precision and nuance of a bunker-buster bomb; the plunge or rise of the generic ballot.

I get it. I was the chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee for two cycles, 2012 and 2014. The 30 days before each election were not only hair-graying, they were hair-raising.

The popular narrative is set: the Democrats are expected to flip the House and have a possible shot in the Senate. But beneath that narrative are fundamental elements that shouldn’t be overlooked. Here are five key takeaways that should guide an informed analysis over the next 30 days.

First, focus on the battlefield, which is dynamic. According to the Cook Political Report (which I find the most credible in capturing the midterm state of play), there are currently 22 pure toss-up seats in the House: six held by Democrats and 16 held by Republicans. You can widen the aperture to another 11 districts that lean Democratic and ten that lean Republican. In other words, the next House majority is likely to turn on the outcome in just 43 districts.

The Senate tells a different story. Cook rates six Republican-held Senate seats as toss-ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas) and one Democratic-held seat (Michigan). Add to that a lean-Democratic seat in New Hampshire, and you have the entirety of the Senate battlefield. The Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the majority, so they must overperform on election night.

Second, disregard the polls and study the trends. For the past several weeks, a bleak environment for Republicans has steadily shifted races toward the Democrats. Last week, Cook moved 15 race ratings in the Democrats’ favor . In a domino cascade, four “Solid Republican” districts moved to “Likely Republican”; six “Likely Republican” districts moved to “Lean Republican”; three “Lean Republican” districts moved to “Toss-Up”; and two “Toss-Up” districts moved to “Lean Democratic.”

Third, what’s driving the erosion for Republicans is best explained in two words: Donald Trump. His numbers are, at least at the moment, an anchor weighing down Republicans, particularly in competitive districts. According to a Cook survey, Trump’s job approval in those districts is at the levels of kryptonite: 42 percent approve and 58 percent disapprove.

But here’s a more interesting and initially misleading indicator: the generic ballot favors the Democrats in those districts by only 2 points (49 percent to 47 percent). Seems tight, until you understand that it has swung 7 points toward Democrats since last year and that Trump carried those same districts by an average of 5 points.

Why is this happening? Three groups of voters in competitive districts are shaping the current political environment. First, there’s the Democratic base, which is supercharged. Enthusiasm among Democrats to vote against Trump Republicans is at the level of nuclear energy. Second, there’s the Republican base, which presents its own challenges. According to a recent Reuters/Ipsos survey, 73 percent of Republican voters approve of Trump . Not bad — but down about 13 points since January. I’m not suggesting that these voters will support a Democrat in the midterms, but some may simply stay home.

The third group is of independent and swing voters. They often resist ideological extremes; they punish Republicans and Democrats alike when they believe they’ve gone too far. They support checks and balances. Trump’s approval among them has been averaging in the high 20s to mid-30s. If you can’t energize your base and independent voters are leaning hard against you, it’s hard to find enough persuadable voters to win in these districts.

Fourth, there’s a silver lining for Republicans in the thunderous sky: money. According to The New Republic, the party has spent or booked $454 million on House races , compared Democrats’ $381 million. In the first three weeks of September, Republicans outspent Democrats by more than $100 million in the seven toss-up Senate races. The question is: will money be enough to convince voters that prices are low, the economy is fine and the war in Iran isn’t a problem? Money in a ground game could help Republicans in districts whose outcome may rest on a few thousand votes. But for many voters, the election is baked in already.

Fifth — remember your history. Midterms are always a referendum on the president and his party. In only a handful of midterms — notably 1934, 1998 and 2002 — has a sitting president’s party picked up House seats.

The next 30 days have the potential for all sorts of crises. But history and the current political environment suggest that Democrats are strongly favored to flip the House … and maybe even the Senate.

Steve Israel represented New York in the House of Representatives for eight terms and was chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee from 2011 to 2015.

articles.title: Ben Affleck slams ‘snarky,’ ‘depressing’ political climate: ‘I think it would be an awful job’
articles.summary: Ben Affleck says running for public office “has no appeal” to him because he finds the political world “very depressing.” The “Gone Girl” star, who plays a Los Angeles mayoral candidate in his new movie “Animals,” shot down talk of making a real-life jump from Hollywood to the campaign trail in an interview with Variety…
articles.body:
Ben Affleck says running for public office “has no appeal” to him because he finds the political world “very depressing.”

The “Gone Girl” star, who plays a Los Angeles mayoral candidate in his new movie “Animals,” shot down talk of making a real-life jump from Hollywood to the campaign trail in an interview with Variety published Wednesday.

“I just think that’s enormously — I don’t know, man, that seems terrible,” Affleck replied when asked if he would ever consider a political bid.

“There’s a reason why political stories are often chosen as parables for moral compromise,” the 54-year-old Academy Award winner said.

“You really get thrust up into the contrast between the ideal version of us and how we should be in our lives and the way it is. It’s a very depressing world, in my opinion,” Affleck said.

“Tawdry,” he added, “And that has no appeal to me.”

Affleck went further into his disdain for politics in an interview with USA Today this week, saying, “On a personal level, I think it would be an awful job.”

“I think the way it’s constructed now is so geared around money and now even geared around like soundbites, and cruelties, and gotchas, and little snarky things that really have nothing to do with people’s lives whatsoever,” the performer said.

“It’s easier to get votes appealing to the worst in people than it is appealing to the best in them,” he said.

“There are lots of pressures that are constantly asking you to sacrifice your principles — and frankly, at this point I think too many — which is why it’s sort of a self-selecting job,” Affleck said.

“And we end up getting people with whom the electorate is perennially dissatisfied because if you get past the sort of party affiliation notions or the tribal notions and you just ask people broadly, ‘Hey, what do you think about the political world and how do you think it’s working?’ there’s a resounding kind of rejection from people, no matter who they may have voted for,” he said.

It’s not the first time that Affleck, who’s long stirred buzz of a possible political run, has expressed dissatisfaction with what’s happening in Washington.

“God, the political climate,” he said in 2016 . “There is little more that I find more depressing than the political climate these days.”

articles.title: Sand holds 12-point lead over Lahn for Iowa governor while Hinson trails Turek in Senate race: Poll
articles.summary: The Democratic candidates for Senate and governor in Iowa are leading in their races, according to a new poll. In the Suffolk University poll, 48 percent of respondents said Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek was their “first choice” if the election occurred that day, with 44 percent saying the same of Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa),…
articles.body:
The Democratic candidates for Senate and governor in Iowa are leading in their races , according to a new poll.

In the Suffolk University poll , 48 percent of respondents said Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek was their “first choice” if the election occurred that day, with 44 percent saying the same of Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa), his GOP opponent. Turek’s lead falls within the survey’s margin of error.

Thomas Laehn, a Libertarian candidate, garnered 2 percent backing, while 6 percent were unsure about their choice and 1 percent did not respond.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The Suffolk poll also found that 55 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand or were leaning toward doing so if the election occurred that day. Forty-three percent said the same of Sand’s Republican opponent, Zach Lahn, and 2 percent were unsure about their choice in the race to replace retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds (R).

Lahn and Sand clashed in their first televised debate Tuesday night, with three more scheduled before Election Day.

According to the National Governors Association , the last time a Democrat held the governorship of the Hawkeye State was 15 years ago , with Gov. Chet Culver. And on the senatorial side, Iowa’s last Democratic senator was Tom Harkin, who left office in 2015 .

Iowa has been a reliably red state within the last decade, with President Trump carrying it in all three of his presidential runs . However, the national electoral environment appears to be better for Democrats these midterms, with polls leaning their way and Republicans dealing with issues like the unpopular Iran war, Trump’s sagging approval rating and concerns about the cost of living.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Iowa governor’s race as leaning Democratic and the Senate race as a toss-up.

The Suffolk University poll took place Oct. 1-4 among 500 registered voters in Iowa and had 4.4 percentage points as its margin of error.
