articles.title: Imperiled House Democrat gets ripped by left and right after flip-flop on transgender sports
articles.summary: Marcy Kaptur faces attacks from both Republicans and progressives over her campaign ads opposing transgender youth in girls sports and schools.
articles.body: One of the most vulnerable House Democrats of the 2026 election cycle is being hammered from the left and right for her stance on transgender youth. Longtime Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is facing one of her toughest re-election battles yet, partially thanks to Buckeye State Republicans redrawing the boundaries of her district to include more GOP voters. In what appears to be an appeal to those voters, Kaptur recently sent out mailers touting her opposition to biological males playing on girls' school sports teams. "Unlike the far left, I believe boys shouldn't play girls' sports," the mailed campaign ad, obtained by Fox News Digital, said. The other side touted that Kaptur "voted to ban schools from touting gender ideology in classrooms." VULNERABLE DEMOCRATS FLIP ON WOMEN'S SPORTS VOTE AFTER OPPOSING SIMILAR BILLS AS MIDTERMS LOOM The moderate Ohio Democrat was referring to her vote in May of this year in favor of the Stopping Indoctrination and Protecting Kids Act, which would condition federal funding to public elementary and middle schools on those schools obtaining parents' permission before any sex or gender accommodations for students are made. POWERFUL LGBTQ+ GROUP'S ENDORSEMENTS COULD TANK VULNERABLE DEMS OVER RADICAL YOUTH TRANS AGENDA She also referenced that vote in a campaign ad, in which she said, "I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools, because parents know best for their kids. And boys should not play in girls' sports." House Republicans' campaign arm pointed out, however, that Kaptur is also a supporter of the Equality Act. That bill, introduced in April 2025, includes language to prohibit public schools from discriminating based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Kaptur is a co-sponsor of the bill. VULNERABLE DEM'S CAMPAIGN PITCH CLASHES WITH 'RADICAL' VOTING RECORD ON TOP CULTURE WAR ISSUE She also voted against the GOP-led Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act in April 2023 and January 2025. The former instance received no Democratic support, while two Democrats voted with Republicans on the bill last year. "Lies from desperate Democrat Marcy Kaptur can't erase her radical record. Kaptur is in damage control, and she must remove herself as a co-sponsor of the Equality Act and disavow her previous votes or remove her lies from the airwaves," National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) spokesman Zach Bannon told Fox News Digital. That stance is creating political headaches for Kaptur on the other side of the aisle, as well. Ohio progressives are accusing Kaptur of throwing transgender kids under the bus to score electoral points. LGBTQ advocacy group Equality Ohio graded Kaptur a "D" for having "recently released anti-trans ads." Lucas County Stonewall Democrats wrote in an open letter to Kaptur, "Shame on you and your campaign staff for pushing this incredibly harmful anti-Trans rhetoric." And an opinion piece in the Buckeye Flame, an LGBTQ news site, stated, "[A]s a 27-year-old working journalist who challenges oppression and interrogates transphobia daily, I am embarrassed at Rep. Kaptur’s name on my resume. So much so that I removed it." Kaptur has survived prior redistricting bids by Republicans to serve her Toledo-area district for over four decades. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But in an election cycle where turning out the base matters to both sides, it's not clear what kind of effect her position on the issue will have. Fox News Digital reached out to Kaptur's campaign but did not receive a response.

articles.title: Hegseth greets ship returning from troubled waters
articles.summary: Plus: 🏒Ovechkin’s final home opener in DC {beacon} It’s Wednesday, and there is no shortage of news coming to us today… In today’s issue: Hegseth greets crew from USS Abraham Lincoln Hinson and Turek debate in Iowa Vance comments on Iran nuclear negotiations Ovechkin’s final home opener in D.C. Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail…
articles.body:
It’s Wednesday, and there is no shortage of news coming to us today…

Hegseth greets crew from USS Abraham Lincoln

Vance comments on Iran nuclear negotiations

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

👨‍⚖️ Join The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams on The Gavel as they unpack the first week of the new Supreme Court term — including Monday’s climate argument and Justice Samuel Alito ‘s new book. Hill Insiders can join the live discussion at 3 p.m. EDT.

Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Brian M. Wilbur, U.S. Navy via AP, File

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth today will greet the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which will return to the U.S. this week following its lengthy deployment in the Middle East.

As The Hill’s Filip Timotija reports : “According to the Pentagon, Hegseth will speak with the ship’s crew, participate in physical training and eat lunch with the service members while in San Diego.”

The Lincoln departed San Diego in November and spent more than 280 days without returning to port.

Democrats in Congress demanded answers following reports of poor conditions and mental health crises on board this summer.

Trump administration pushed back: “Listen, we make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” Hegseth said in August, adding that “some deployments are longer than others.”

“The rampant misreporting on Abraham Lincoln’s historic deployment is a disservice to our men and women in uniform and their loved ones,” U.S. Central Command, which oversaw the mission, wrote in an August social media post on X.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the media’s claims of mistreatment were “trying to paint our warriors as victims.”

The Pentagon plans to expand missions targeting drug cartels in South America.

U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan spoke with The Hill about Southcom’s objectives, particularly its “Offensive Campaign Plan.”

“Based on our assessment of what needs to be done, this plan focuses on five core lines of effort: dismantling illicit networks, attacking network logistics, preventing adversary regeneration, bolstering partner sovereignty and security, and building a strong coalition,” Donovan said in the interview.

For over a year, the U.S. military has been striking small vessels it deemed drug boats. In a recent escalation, the Trump administration put American forces on the ground in Ecuador to collaborate with local authorities and take down traffickers the U.S. now labels as foreign terrorist organizations.

One successful attack allegedly killed a Tren de Aragua gang leader.

A senior Pentagon official who spoke on the condition of anonymity told The Hill, “That’s kind of like a graduation of how we’ve been able to work with that country, but certainly not the endpoint. Just kind of like progress along the way. So I think you will expect to see more operations, especially as capabilities begin to start to develop.”

The same official added that Guatemala and Honduras have inquired about similar joint missions.

A night after Iowa’s gubernatorial candidates, Zach Lahn (R) and Rob Sand (D), duked it out on the debate stage, the Hawkeye State’s highly contested Senate race will be in the spotlight Wednesday night.

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) is set to go up against Democratic opponent Josh Turek in a state that has seen the lead dwindle for Republicans, according to recent polling.

What to watch for: As of late, Hinson has distanced herself from President Trump due to frustrations among Iowans surrounding high gas and grocery prices.

In September, Hinson wanted the House to return to session “immediately” over the rising diesel prices thanks to the Iran war — another subject that has split the GOP Senate candidate and Trump.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Hinson wrote on social media.

All talk on Turek: No Democrat has won a Senate seat in Iowa since Sen. Tom Harkin in 2008, and no presidential candidate has won the state since former President Obama in 2012.

But Turek has received Obama’s endorsement, something that has only happened twice in this election cycle.

A September poll from Marist University shows Turek with an 8-point lead over Hinson, while Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) lists the state as a toss-up.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) will go head-to-head Wednesday night with state Treasurer and Republican candidate Stacy Garrity, a close ally to President Trump.

Mind on measles: Shapiro has made headlines recently over his feud with Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on the state’s measles outbreak.

RFK Jr. accused Shapiro of failing to cooperate with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), igniting a response from the Pennsylvania Democrat.

“Incompetence is letting measles, a disease that was declared eliminated in 2000, reemerge,” Shapiro wrote on the social platform X. “Incompetence is spending your time promoting outright lies instead of urging people to get a vaccination that would protect them against this deadly disease. Incompetence is denying the tragedy of four measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.”

According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health , the state has now recorded over 1,000 cases of measles, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths.

Who supports data centers?: Garrity and Shapiro have released ads targeting one another on protecting data centers.

Garrity’s claimed that Shapiro supported Amazon building data centers in the state last year and bashed the Pennsylvania governor’s 2025 Fast Track data center permitting program. Amazon invested $20 billion in the program to build two facilities in Luzerne and Bucks counties.

At the time of the Fast Track data center program, Garrity said it would be a great thing for the state and create thousands of jobs but has since backtracked her remarks.

Shapiro responded to the ad, saying he will not allow his state to “be bullied by developers and bulldozed by the lawyers” working for these tech companies.

An August poll from New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena has Garrity trailing Shapiro by 15 points.

South Carolina’s 1 st Congressional District : Republican Nancy Honeycutt will face off against Democrat Nancy Lacore for the opportunity to succeed Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.).

Arizona 1 st Congressional District : Former NFL kicker Jay Feely (R) is set to debate former state Rep. Amish Shah (D). The winner in November will succeed GOP Rep. David Schweikert.

Vice President Vance emphasized in an interview with Reuters on Tuesday that Iran must do something “meaningful” related to their enriched uranium to make progress in nuclear negotiations with the U.S.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched ⁠fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said during the interview.

Not doing anything nuclear: According to a report from The Hill’s Laura Kelly, Iran is not looking to build a nuclear weapon with its stockpile of enriched uranium, but the U.S. says otherwise.

“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” Vance said on Iran’s claims.

Leadership questions: Vance noted that Iran’s leadership crisis is another reason no deal has been made, but the country’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei stated, “the problem is actually the opposite.”

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) is urging Russia to provide more details on the recent death of a researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia. Russian authorities say the woman died from severe pneumonia, drawing international concern. But the WHO chief is now pressing the global superpower for answers on the source of the infection.

A record number of books were banned this year, according to a study from PEN America. Between 2025 and 2026, almost 12,000 books were removed from shelves, primarily in Texas and Florida, which removed 8,100 and 3,200, respectively. In Texas, the increase in bans may be driven by a September 2025 law restricting titles deemed sexually explicit or harmful.

The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan , the convicted terrorist in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, has been scheduled for December, according to the U.S. Army. Hasan was convicted of shooting unarmed American soldiers at the base, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) said she was “horrified” by Trump’s remarks at a Monday rally in Nebraska that Iran could “take out” LA and San Diego. “The role of the president is to protect and defend the American people,” Bass told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Tuesday.

articles.title: Boosting public safety starts with fully funding federal prisons
articles.summary: Advocacy leader Scott Peyton argues that Congress must provide the Federal Bureau of Prisons with necessary funding to address critical staffing shortages, maintain facility safety, and support successful reentry programs for incarcerated individuals.
articles.body:
Some self-surrender. Others are put on a bus, bound for the place they will live for a period of time. Upon arrival, the imposing razor wire, high fencing, and unmistakable sound of the gate locking behind them are stark signs that a prison sentence has begun.

Just under half a million people enter prison each year. Many Americans believe the job of public safety ends there, but 95 percent of prisoners will be released. Sadly, two out of three will be rearrested within three years, so we must think about public safety beyond the prison walls.

The stated job of the Federal Bureau of Prisons is to ensure men and women do their time “ in facilities that are safe, humane, cost-efficient, and appropriately secure .” The bureau also offers numerous reentry programs to help people better themselves so they can return home and succeed.

But those aspirations cannot be fulfilled without proper financial support. Congress should fully fund federal prisons so the bureau is adequately staffed and equipped to safely prepare incarcerated men and women for reentry and reduce further instances of crime.

The Bureau of Prisons has a massive footprint, with prisons from Hawaii to New Hampshire and more than 153,000 prisoners in its custody. Just under 34,000 employees work for the agency, but not all are correctional officers. This has led to a dangerously high prisoner-to-officer ratio, which reached 10.2-to-one in 2024 .

Inadequate funding and the resultant low pay for correctional officers, when compared to other law enforcement agencies, have plagued the bureau for years. This has resulted in “pervasive” staffing shortages, according to the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General. In addition, many of the bureau’s facilities are in need of urgent maintenance.

These challenges came to a head in July when the bureau announced multiple prison closures . Despite a $5 billion cash infusion from Congress last year, the bureau conceded it wasn’t enough to solve problems that have lingered for decades.

A lack of adequate resources renders the Bureau of Prisons unable to fulfill its public safety mission. This can be as simple as having enough staff on duty to supervise addiction recovery groups or educational, vocational, and other types of programs like the new Prison Fellowship Academy at Federal Correctional Institution El Reno in Oklahoma. The Prison Fellowship program helps men and women replace criminal thinking and behaviors with renewed values and purpose. Prisoners who participate in educational or vocational training while incarcerated have a 43 percent lower recidivism rate , according to the RAND Corporation.

The safety of those who work and live in prison is of utmost importance. Understaffing makes work dangerous for those who are on duty, and it worsens living conditions for prisoners. This can lead to violence and lockdowns, which leaves the bureau with less time to focus on prisoner rehabilitation and reentry.

The Bureau of Prisons doesn’t determine who goes to prison or how long they stay. Rather, it is the final link in the criminal justice chain — though often the one that gets the least attention. This is not sustainable; when one link is weakened, the entire chain is at risk of collapse.

Funding the bureau may not seem like a high priority, but it is necessary to advance public safety and protect those who work and live in prison. It is also paramount if we want people who serve their time in prison to successfully reintegrate into society.

The pillars of maintaining safe and secure facilities and preparing people for reentry can only be realized if the Bureau of Prisons is provided the necessary resources. Congress must act soon to secure this vital funding.

Scott Peyton is the senior director of advocacy for Prison Fellowship.

articles.title: Tillis backs Whatley in North Carolina Senate race
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is backing Republican candidate Michael Whatley for the Senate seat he’s leaving behind — his first public declaration of who he will support. Whatley is in a tight race against former Gov. Roy Cooper (D), who is currently favored to win. Tillis told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, on Tuesday that…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is backing Republican candidate Michael Whatley for the Senate seat he’s leaving behind — his first public declaration of who he will support.

Whatley is in a tight race against former Gov. Roy Cooper (D), who is currently favored to win . Tillis told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, on Tuesday that he supports Whatley.

“Of course I don’t support Roy Cooper. I support Michael Whatley and every Republican up and down the ticket,” Tillis said. “I think more people should look at how they can help Republicans get elected versus be perfectionists at the expense of getting Republicans elected.”

Tillis has publicly sparred with President Trump over various issues, usually out of concern for Whatley’s campaign.

He has said Whatley should not campaign with Trump given the president’s low approval rating and the need to win over independent voters.

“I don’t think it benefits him. I haven’t seen any poll where [Trump] is going to help us with unaffiliateds,” he said.
